\title{Explore Once, Evaluate Many: Multiple Policy Evaluation for Stochastic Linear Bandits}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}%
We study how to evaluate $K$ target policies simultaneously
in stochastic contextual bandits with linear reward structure.
Given a known $d$-dimensional feature map and reward-free
access to policy queries, we propose PRISMA (Policy evaluation through Regularized
Information Sharing and Mixture Allocation), an algorithm
that estimates every target policy's value to accuracy
$\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$.
The algorithm uses
$\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\!\left(
\frac{(L^2S^2+\beta^2)(1\vee\rho^\star)}{\varepsilon^2} \cdot \log(K)
\right)$ context draws and reward observations,
where $\rho^\star\le d$ is an instance-dependent measure
of the difficulty of designing a shared sampling distribution.
Here, $L$, $S$, and $\beta$ bound the feature norm,
reward parameter norm, and reward noise, respectively,
and the suppressed factors are logarithmic in
$K$, $d$, and $1/\delta$.
Our method combines reward-free planning, a regularized
sampling design, and a single ridge regression estimator
shared across all target policies.
An adaptive doubling procedure selects the regularization
scale without knowledge of $\rho^\star$.
The guarantees require no numerical lower bound on
second-moment eigenvalues and have no explicit dependence
on the cardinalities of the context and action spaces.
Policy-query costs are accounted for separately,
with $K$ queries per shared planning context.
\end{abstract}

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

We studied simultaneous policy evaluation in stochastic
contextual bandits with linear reward structure.
Our results show that reward-free planning and a shared
sampling design yield instance-dependent guarantees
without explicit dependence on the cardinalities of
the context and action spaces or a numerical lower
bound on second-moment eigenvalues.

A natural direction is to extend these techniques to
linear MDPs and more general function approximation settings.
In these settings, an additional challenge is that
the policies influence the distributions of future states,
so feature moments cannot be estimated directly from
a shared policy-independent context distribution.

An open question is whether $\rho\opt$ captures the
intrinsic difficulty of evaluation in the linear setting.
Our analysis provides an upper bound in terms of this
quantity, but does not establish its necessity.
Matching lower bounds would help determine when mixtures
of target policies achieve the optimal evaluation cost
and whether more general sampling strategies can improve
upon them.

\title{Extending the Oracle Approximating Shrinkage to General Distributions}
\author{Michael J. Lewis\\

\begin{abstract}
The Oracle Approximating Shrinkage (OAS) estimator provides a closed-form, data-driven
shrinkage intensity for regularizing sample covariance matrices toward a scaled identity
target, but its derivation assumes Gaussian data.
In practice, financial returns, neural signals, and many other high-dimensional datasets
exhibit heavy tails and non-zero kurtosis, violating this assumption.
We extend OAS to any distribution with finite fourth moments by incorporating a correction
term $\alpha$ built from the fourth-order joint cumulants of the data.
The correction vanishes under Gaussianity, recovering the OAS formula as a special
case; it admits a consistent $O(np)$ sample estimator and satisfies $\rho\in[0,1]$ exactly
for both the population cumulant and its sample analogue.
Simulations and an equity-returns study confirm that the correction closes the gap between
OAS and the Ledoit--Wolf estimator under non-Gaussian data, with OAS-Extended
performing comparably across all tested settings.
The contribution is a principled correction for OAS practitioners facing heavy-tailed data;
structurally, it is distinct from prior work extending Ledoit--Wolf to elliptical
distributions, which optimizes against a fixed oracle target and yields a different
closed-form formula.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec-intro}

Estimating a covariance matrix from data is a fundamental task across a wide range of
disciplines, including portfolio optimization \cite{LW2004}, signal processing \cite{OAS},
and neuroscience.
In the classical low-dimensional regime, the sample covariance matrix $\hat{S}$ is a
consistent and unbiased estimator of the true covariance $\Sigma$.
However, in the modern high-dimensional setting where the number of variables $p$ is
comparable to or exceeds the number of observations $n$, $\hat{S}$ becomes poorly
conditioned or singular, and its eigenvalues are known to be severely dispersed relative
to those of $\Sigma$.

Shrinkage estimators address this by forming a convex combination
\begin{equation*}
\hat{\Sigma} = (1 - \rho)\hat{S} + \rho \hat{F},
\end{equation*}
where $\hat{F}$ is a well-conditioned target matrix and $\rho \in [0,1]$ is a shrinkage
intensity.
The celebrated Ledoit--Wolf (LW) estimator \cite{LW2004} chooses $\rho$ to minimize the
expected Frobenius loss $E[\lVert \hat{\Sigma} - \Sigma \rVert_F^2]$ against the oracle
target $\hat{F} = (\operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma)/p)\,I$.
The Oracle Approximating Shrinkage (OAS) estimator of Chen et al.\ \cite{OAS} takes a
different approach: it uses the data-dependent target
$\hat{F} = (\operatorname{Tr}(\hat{S})/p)\,I$ and derives $\rho$ via a fixed-point
iteration that converges to a closed-form expression.
This distinction --- random versus fixed target --- leads to structurally different
formulas and different finite-sample behavior, with OAS typically outperforming LW
at small $n/p$ ratios under Gaussian data.

Both estimators were originally derived under the assumption that the data are drawn from
a multivariate Gaussian distribution.
In many practical settings this assumption fails.
Financial asset returns are well-documented to exhibit excess kurtosis and heavy tails.
More broadly, any distribution in the elliptical family --- including the multivariate
Student-$t$ --- introduces fourth-order cumulant structure that the Gaussian-derived
formulas ignore.
Under such heavy-tailed distributions, applying the OAS formula amounts to a misspecified
estimator, and the resulting shrinkage intensity is suboptimal.

The key insight is that the Gaussian derivation of OAS depends on two expectations ---
$E[\operatorname{Tr}(\hat{S}^2)]$ and $E[\operatorname{Tr}^2(\hat{S})]$ --- each of which
acquires an additional term $\alpha/n$ under a general distribution, where
$\alpha = \sum_{i,j} \kappa(X_i, X_i, X_j, X_j)$ aggregates the fourth-order joint
cumulants of the data.
Incorporating this term propagates through the fixed-point iteration and yields a
corrected closed-form shrinkage intensity that reduces to the OAS formula when
$\alpha = 0$.
We also provide a consistent sample estimator $\hat{\alpha}$ and prove that the corrected
formula preserves $\rho \in [0,1]$ for both the population cumulant and the sample
estimator, so an OAS practitioner facing non-Gaussian data can adopt the extended
formula without changing frameworks.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows.
Section~\ref{sec-related} discusses related work, with particular attention to the

Section~\ref{sec-formulation} derives the corrected oracle shrinkage intensity.
Section~\ref{sec-extension} derives OAS-Extended and its closed form.
Section~\ref{sec-simulation} presents a Monte Carlo simulation study comparing

Section~\ref{sec-financial} applies all estimators to a rolling-window study on
daily returns of $p=50$ large-cap US equities.
Section~\ref{sec-conclusion} concludes.
The proof that $\rho \in [0,1]$ is given in the Appendix.

\section{Related Work}\label{sec-related}

The closest prior work to this paper is the line of research by Ollila and collaborators
on extending Ledoit--Wolf (LW) shrinkage \cite{LW2004} to elliptical distributions
\cite{Ollila2017, OllilaRaninen2019, Ollila2023}.
In those works, the oracle shrinkage intensity minimizes
$E\left[\lVert (1-\rho)\hat{S} + \rho\mu I - \Sigma \rVert_F^2\right]$
where $\mu = \operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma)/p$ is a \emph{fixed} oracle scalar, yielding a
closed-form expression parameterized by the scalar elliptical kurtosis $\kappa$ and the
sphericity $\gamma = p\operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma^2)/\operatorname{Tr}^2(\Sigma)$.

The OAS framework of \cite{OAS}, which the present work extends, differs from LW in a
structurally important way: the shrinkage target is
$\hat{F} = (\operatorname{Tr}(\hat{S})/p)\,I$, a \emph{random, data-dependent} quantity
rather than the oracle $\mu I$.
This changes the optimization problem and produces a different formula via a fixed-point
iteration; the two approaches are not equivalent even in the Gaussian case.
Consequently, the elliptical-distribution results of \cite{Ollila2017, OllilaRaninen2019}
do not imply an extension of OAS, and to the best of our knowledge the present work is
the first to provide one.

Beyond the structural distinction, our result is also more general in distributional scope.
The Ollila line of work restricts to elliptical distributions, for which the fourth-order
cumulant collapses to a single scalar parameter $\kappa$ via
$\kappa(X_i, X_i, X_j, X_j) = \kappa\bigl(\Sigma_{ii}\Sigma_{jj} + 2\Sigma_{ij}^2\bigr)$.
Our result holds for any distribution with finite fourth moments, where the aggregate cumulant
$\alpha = \sum_{i,j} \kappa(X_i, X_i, X_j, X_j)$ need not have this constrained form.
Elliptical distributions are thus a special case of our framework.

\section{Formulation}\label{sec-formulation}

\paragraph{Setup and notation.}
Let $X^1, \ldots, X^n \in \mathbb{R}^p$ be independent and identically distributed draws
from a centered distribution with covariance matrix $\Sigma$, i.e.\ $E[X^k] = 0$ and
$E[X^k (X^k)^T] = \Sigma$.
We assume the distribution has finite fourth moments.
The index $X_i^k$ denotes the $i$-th component of the $k$-th sample.
The sample covariance matrix is
\begin{equation*}
\hat{S} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^n X^k (X^k)^T,
\end{equation*}
and the shrinkage target is the scaled identity $\hat{F} = \frac{\operatorname{Tr}(\hat{S})}{p} I$,
whose scale is chosen to match the average eigenvalue of $\hat{S}$.
Throughout, $p$ denotes the dimension and $n$ the number of observations.
All expectations are taken over the distribution of the samples.

The setup, notation, and following equations follow \cite{OAS} and serve as our starting point.
\begin{equation}
\rho_O = \frac{ E \left[ \operatorname{Tr} \left( \left( \Sigma - \hat{S} \right) \left( \hat{F} - \hat{S} \right) \right) \right] }{ E \left[ \lVert \hat{S} - \hat{F} \rVert_F^2 \right] }
\end{equation}
\begin{multline}
E \left[ \operatorname{Tr} \left( \left( \Sigma - \hat{S} \right) \left( \hat{F} - \hat{S} \right) \right) \right] =
\frac{\operatorname{Tr}( \Sigma )}{p} E \left[ \operatorname{Tr}(\hat{S})\right]
- \frac{ E \left[ \operatorname{Tr}^2(\hat{S})\right] }{ p } \\
- E \left[ \operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma \hat{S})\right]
+ E \left[ \operatorname{Tr}(\hat{S}^2)\right]
\end{multline}
\begin{equation}
E \left[ \lVert \hat{S} - \hat{F} \rVert_F^2 \right] =
E \left[ \operatorname{Tr}(\hat{S}^2)\right]
- \frac{ E \left[ \operatorname{Tr}^2(\hat{S})\right] }{ p }
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
E \left[ \operatorname{Tr}(\hat{S})\right] = \operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma)
\end{equation}
Here we depart from \cite{OAS}: rather than assuming Gaussianity, we allow the
distribution to be arbitrary with finite fourth moments.
Observe that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
E \left[ \operatorname{Tr}(\hat{S}^2)\right] &= E \left[ \lVert \hat{S} \rVert_F^2 \right] \\
&= \sum_{i,j} \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{k,l} E \left[ X_i^k X_j^k X_i^l X_j^l \right] \\
&= \sum_{i,j} \frac{1}{n^2} \left( \sum_{k \neq l} E \left[ X_i^k X_j^k X_i^l X_j^l \right] + \sum_{k = l} E \left[ X_i^k X_j^k X_i^l X_j^l \right] \right) \\
&= \frac{n-1}{n} \sum_{i,j} \Sigma^2_{i,j} + \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{i,j} \sum_k E \left[ (X_i^k)^2 (X_j^k)^2 \right] \\
&= \frac{n-1}{n} \operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma^2) + \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i,j} E \left[ X_i^2 X_j^2 \right] \\
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
Similarly,
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
E \left[ \operatorname{Tr}^2(\hat{S})\right] &= E \left[ \sum_{i,j} \hat{S}_{ii} \hat{S}_{jj} \right] \\
&= \sum_{i,j} \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{k,l} E \left[  (X_i^k)^2  (X_j^l)^2  \right] \\
&= \sum_{i,j} \frac{1}{n^2} \left( \sum_{k \neq l} E \left[  (X_i^k)^2  (X_j^l)^2  \right] + \sum_{k = l} E \left[  (X_i^k)^2  (X_j^l)^2  \right] \right) \\
&= \frac{n-1}{n} \sum_{i,j} \Sigma_{ii} \Sigma_{jj} + \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{i,j} \sum_k E \left[ (X_i^k)^2  (X_j^k)^2 \right] \\
&= \frac{n-1}{n} \operatorname{Tr}^2(\Sigma) + \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i,j} E \left[ X_i^2  X_j^2 \right] \\
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
The term $E \left[ X_i^2  X_j^2 \right]$ appears in both expansions.
For a centered distribution with finite fourth moments,
\begin{equation}
E \left[ X_i^2  X_j^2 \right] = \Sigma_{ii} \Sigma_{jj} + 2 \Sigma_{ij}^2 + \kappa( X_i, X_i, X_j, X_j )
\end{equation}
where $\kappa( X_i, X_i, X_j, X_j )$ represents the fourth-order joint cumulant.
This cumulant vanishes identically under Gaussianity.
Thus,
\begin{equation}
\label{fourth_moment_eqn}
\sum_{i,j} E \left[ X_i^2  X_j^2 \right] = \operatorname{Tr}^2(\Sigma) + 2 \operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma^2) + \sum_{i,j} \kappa( X_i, X_i, X_j, X_j )
\end{equation}
Let $\alpha =\sum_{i,j} \kappa( X_i, X_i, X_j, X_j )$.

Substituting \eqref{fourth_moment_eqn} into the expansions above,
\begin{equation}
E \left[ \operatorname{Tr}(\hat{S}^2)\right] = \frac{n+1}{n} \operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma^2) + \frac{1}{n} \operatorname{Tr}^2(\Sigma) + \frac{\alpha}{n}
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
E \left[ \operatorname{Tr}^2(\hat{S})\right] = \operatorname{Tr}^2(\Sigma) + \frac{2}{n} \operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma^2) + \frac{\alpha}{n}
\end{equation}
which match the Gaussian results of \cite{OAS} up to the additional $\frac{\alpha}{n}$ term.
Substituting into the oracle formula and simplifying yields the corrected oracle intensity:
\begin{equation}
\label{opt_rho}
\rho_O = \frac{ (1-2/p) \operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma^2) + \operatorname{Tr}^2(\Sigma) + \alpha (1 - 1/p) }{ (n+1-2/p) \operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma^2) + (1 - n/p) \operatorname{Tr}^2(\Sigma) + \alpha (1 - 1/p) }
\end{equation}

\section{Extending OAS}\label{sec-extension}
We now apply the OAS fixed-point framework of \cite{OAS} to the corrected oracle formula \eqref{opt_rho}.
As in \cite{OAS}, we have
\begin{equation}
\label{rho_eval}
\hat{\rho}_{j+1} = \frac{ (1-2/p) \operatorname{Tr}(\hat{\Sigma}_j \hat{S} ) + \operatorname{Tr}^2( \hat{\Sigma}_j ) + \alpha (1 - 1/p) }{ (n+1-2/p) \operatorname{Tr}( \hat{\Sigma}_j \hat{S} ) + (1 - n/p) \operatorname{Tr}^2( \hat{\Sigma}_j ) + \alpha (1 - 1/p) } \\
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
\label{sigma_eval}
\hat{\Sigma}_{j+1} = (1 - \hat{\rho}_{j+1}) \hat{S} + \hat{\rho}_{j+1} \hat{F} \\
\end{equation}
which leverages \eqref{opt_rho}, but replaces $\operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma)$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma^2)$ with
$\operatorname{Tr}(\hat{\Sigma}_j)$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(\hat{\Sigma}_j \hat{S})$, respectively.
Let
\begin{equation}
\hat{\phi} = \frac{ \operatorname{Tr}( \hat{S}^2 ) - \operatorname{Tr}^2( \hat{S} ) / p }{ (1-2/p) \operatorname{Tr}( \hat{S}^2 ) + \operatorname{Tr}^2( \hat{S} ) } = \frac{ \operatorname{Tr}( \hat{S}^2 ) - \operatorname{Tr}^2( \hat{S} ) / p }{ M }
\end{equation}
and $\beta = \alpha (1 -  1/p) / M$.
Substituting \eqref{sigma_eval} into \eqref{rho_eval} and simplifying yields
\begin{equation}
\hat{\rho}_{j+1} = \frac{ 1 + \beta - (1 - 2/p) \hat{\phi} \hat{\rho}_j }{ 1 + \beta + n \hat{\phi} - (n+1-2/p) \hat{\phi} \hat{\rho}_j }
\end{equation}
Using the change of variables
\begin{equation}
b_j  = \frac{1}{ 1 + \beta - (n+1-2/p) \hat{\phi} \hat{\rho}_j } \Leftrightarrow \hat{\rho}_j = \frac{ 1 + \beta - \frac{1}{b_j} }{ (n+1-2/p) \hat{\phi} },
\end{equation}
showing that \eqref{rho_eval} is equivalent to
\begin{equation}
b_{j+1} =  \frac{  n \hat{\phi} }{ 1 + \beta - (1-2/p) \hat{\phi} } b_j + \frac{ 1 }{  1 + \beta - (1-2/p) \hat{\phi} }
\end{equation}
Since this is a linear recurrence in $b_j$, its limit is
\begin{equation}
  \lim_{j \to \infty} b_j =
    \begin{cases}
      \infty & \frac{  n \hat{\phi} }{ 1 + \beta - (1-2/p) \hat{\phi} } \geq  1 \\
      \frac{1}{1 + \beta - (n+1-2/p) \hat{\phi} }      & \frac{  n \hat{\phi} }{ 1 + \beta - (1-2/p) \hat{\phi} } < 1 \\
    \end{cases}
\end{equation}
This implies
\begin{equation}
  \lim_{j \to \infty} \hat{\rho}_j =
    \begin{cases}
      \frac{ 1 + \beta }{ (n+1-2/p) \hat{\phi} } & (n+1-2/p) \hat{\phi} \geq 1 + \beta \\
      1                                          & (n+1-2/p) \hat{\phi} < 1 + \beta \\
    \end{cases}
\end{equation}
or equivalently,
\begin{equation}
\label{new_OAS}
\rho_{\text{OAS-Extended}} = \min\left( 1, \frac{ 1 + \beta }{ (n+1-2/p) \hat{\phi} } \right)
\end{equation}

That $1 + \beta \geq 0$ is established in Appendix~\ref{app:proof}, ensuring $\rho_{\text{OAS-Extended}} \geq 0$,
so \eqref{new_OAS} defines a valid shrinkage intensity in $[0,1]$.

It remains to construct a consistent estimator for $\beta$.
Since $M = (1-2/p) \operatorname{Tr}( \hat{S}^2 ) + \operatorname{Tr}^2( \hat{S} )$ is computable from $\hat{S}$, it suffices to estimate $\alpha$.
By its definition and \eqref{fourth_moment_eqn}, the natural estimator is
\begin{equation}
\hat{\alpha} = \left( \sum_{i,j} \frac{1}{n} \sum_k (X_i^k)^2 (X_j^k)^2 \right) - \operatorname{Tr}^2(\hat{S}) - 2 \operatorname{Tr}(\hat{S}^2),
\end{equation}
which converges to the true $\alpha$ by the law of large numbers.
Noting that $\sum_{i,j}\frac{1}{n}\sum_k (X_i^k)^2(X_j^k)^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_k \lVert X^k \rVert^4$
and $\operatorname{Tr}(\hat{S}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_k \lVert X^k \rVert^2$, the estimator simplifies to
\begin{equation}
\hat{\alpha} = \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}\!\left(\lVert X \rVert^2\right) - 2\operatorname{Tr}(\hat{S}^2),
\end{equation}
where $\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\lVert X \rVert^2) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_k \lVert X^k \rVert^4 - \operatorname{Tr}^2(\hat{S})$
is the sample variance of the squared norms.
This form has a natural interpretation: $\hat{\alpha}$ measures the excess squared-norm
variance beyond what a Gaussian with covariance $\hat{S}$ would produce
($2\operatorname{Tr}(\hat{S}^2)$ being the Gaussian value), and is computable in $O(np)$
additional time once $\hat{S}$ is formed.
Substituting $\hat{\beta}$ for $\beta$ in \eqref{new_OAS} gives the sample estimator.
Appendix~\ref{app:proof} shows that $1 + \hat{\beta} \geq 0$ holds exactly for
every finite sample, so $\hat{\rho}_{\text{OAS-Extended}} \in [0,1]$ without any clamping.

\section{Simulation Study}\label{sec-simulation}

We evaluate OAS-Extended against four competitors: OAS \cite{OAS},
the Rao-Blackwell Ledoit--Wolf (RBLW) estimator \cite{OAS},
the analytical Ledoit--Wolf (LW) estimator \cite{LW2004}, and the
sample covariance matrix.
All experiments use a $p=120$ dimensional AR(1) covariance structure
$\Sigma_{ij} = 0.5^{|i-j|}$, with $n/p \in \{0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 5\}$ and 500 independent
trials per setting.
The smallest ratio $n/p = 0.25$ corresponds to $n = 30$ observations, ensuring the
sample is large enough for stable estimation of $\hat{\alpha}$ while remaining well
into the high-dimensional regime where $\hat{S}$ is singular.
Performance is measured by the normalized Frobenius loss
$\lVert \hat{\Sigma} - \Sigma \rVert_F / \lVert \Sigma \rVert_F$.

Three distributions are considered.
The Gaussian case ($\alpha = 0$) serves as a sanity check.
We then draw from a multivariate Student-$t$ with $\nu = 10$ degrees of freedom
(excess kurtosis $= 1$) and $\nu = 5$ (excess kurtosis $= 6$),
both scaled so that $\operatorname{Cov}(X) = \Sigma$ exactly.
Both choices satisfy $\nu > 4$, the requirement for finite fourth moments.
For a multivariate Student-$t$ with $\nu$ degrees of freedom, the elliptical family
formula gives $\alpha = \frac{2}{\nu-4}\bigl[\operatorname{Tr}^2(\Sigma) + 2\operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma^2)\bigr]$,
which grows rapidly as $\nu$ decreases toward 4, explaining why the $\alpha$ correction
is substantially larger under $t(\nu\!=\!5)$ than $t(\nu\!=\!10)$.

Table~\ref{tab:sim} reports mean losses.
Under Gaussian data all four shrinkage estimators perform comparably (confirming no bias
when $\alpha = 0$), with the minor exception of $n/p = 0.25$ where $\hat{\alpha}$
estimation noise marginally inflates OAS-Extended's intensity; this gap closes by
$n/p = 0.5$.
Under non-Gaussian data, four findings stand out.
First, the correction recovers the performance lost by OAS's Gaussian
misspecification: OAS-Extended performs comparably to LW, with differences small at
$n/p = 0.25$ and negligible at $n/p \geq 1$.
Second, both dominate OAS substantially under $t(\nu\!=\!5)$: losses fall
by 46--48\% at $n/p \leq 0.5$, $\sim$36\% at $n/p = 1$, $\sim$24\% at $n/p = 2$, and $\sim$16\% at $n/p = 5$.
Third, RBLW performs comparably to OAS under non-Gaussian data and in some
settings is slightly worse, confirming that neither the Rao-Blackwell construction of
RBLW nor the fixed-point iteration of OAS provides a non-Gaussian correction.
Fourth, the improvement of OAS-Extended over OAS grows with kurtosis and
shrinks as $n/p$ increases, exactly as predicted by the theory.

\section{Empirical Study: Financial Returns}\label{sec-financial}

We complement the Monte Carlo evidence with an application to daily equity returns.
The universe consists of $p = 50$ large-cap US equities drawn from the S\&P~500 index;
we use adjusted daily log-returns from January 2010 to December 2023
($T = 3{,}521$ trading days), downloaded via the \texttt{yfinance} library.
Returns are demeaned within each estimation window.

\paragraph{Rolling-window evaluation.}
We adopt a rolling-window protocol with in-sample window $T_{\mathrm{in}} = 252$ trading
days (approximately one trading year, giving $n/p \approx 5$) and an out-of-sample
horizon of 21 trading days (one calendar month), stepped forward monthly, yielding
$N = 155$ evaluation windows.
At each step we estimate the covariance matrix with each of the five estimators and form
the global minimum variance (GMV) portfolio $\hat{w} \propto \hat{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{1}$.
Performance is measured by the mean annualized realized volatility
$100\% \times \sqrt{252 \cdot \overline{\operatorname{Var}(\hat{w}^{\!\top} r_{\mathrm{out}})}}$.

\paragraph{Non-Gaussianity.}
Figure~\ref{fig:financial} (left) plots $\hat{\alpha}$ over the 155 rolling windows.
The estimate is positive in every window (median $\hat{\alpha} = 9.0 \times 10^{-5}$,
mean $6.5 \times 10^{-4}$), confirming the well-documented heavy-tailed character of
equity returns.
The largest values coincide with periods of elevated market stress; the spike in early 2020
corresponds to the COVID-19 market dislocation.

\paragraph{Portfolio results.}
Table~\ref{tab:financial} reports mean annualized realized volatility for each estimator.
OAS-Extended reduces realized volatility by 2.0\% relative to OAS
(13.28\% vs.\ 13.55\%), approaching LW (13.282\% vs.\ 13.276\%),
consistent with the simulation findings.
RBLW closely tracks OAS (13.55\%), again mirroring the Monte Carlo results.
The improvement of OAS-Extended over OAS is highly significant
($t = 3.83$, $p < 0.001$; bootstrap 95\% CI for the mean variance reduction:
$[2.0, 5.0] \times 10^{-6}$).
LW achieves the same significance ($t = 3.85$, $p < 0.001$).
RBLW also reaches formal significance ($t = 3.88$, $p < 0.001$), but its mean variance
reduction is below $10^{-7}$ --- more than 30 times smaller than OAS-Extended's ---
and the bootstrap 95\% CI rounds to zero at six decimal places.
The result is statistically detectable but economically negligible, confirming that
neither RBLW nor OAS provides a meaningful non-Gaussian correction.

\paragraph{Regime breakdown.}
We classify each window as \emph{stress} if the mean VIX over the in-sample period
exceeds 20 (a standard threshold for elevated implied volatility), and \emph{calm}
otherwise.
Of the 155 windows, 99 are calm and 56 are stress.
Table~\ref{tab:regime} and Figure~\ref{fig:financial} (right) report the improvement
over OAS by regime.
In calm windows the correction yields a 1.0\% vol reduction.
In stress windows the improvement rises to 4.0\%, approximately four times larger.
This concentration of the gain in high-$\hat{\alpha}$ periods is the direct
empirical counterpart of the theory: when heavy-tailed behavior is most pronounced,
the correction to the shrinkage intensity matters most.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec-conclusion}

We have derived a closed-form correction to the Oracle Approximating Shrinkage estimator
valid for any distribution with finite fourth moments.
The correction enters through a single scalar $\alpha$ aggregating the fourth-order joint
cumulants of the data; it vanishes under Gaussianity, recovering the OAS formula
as a special case.
A consistent $O(np)$ sample estimator $\hat{\alpha}$ is available in closed form, and the
corrected shrinkage intensity lies in $[0,1]$ exactly for both the population cumulant and
its sample analogue.

Simulations and a rolling-window equity study confirm that the correction closes the gap
between OAS and Ledoit--Wolf under heavy-tailed data, with gains largest at small
$n/p$ and in high-stress market regimes.
The correction itself requires only finite fourth moments and applies to real-world data
regardless of parametric form.
The simulation study is, however, limited to Student-$t$ distributions and an AR(1)
covariance structure, and the financial application covers a single universe of US
large-cap equities; generalization of the empirical findings to other settings remains
to be assessed.
Natural extensions include applying the framework to structured shrinkage targets such as
factor models or banded covariance matrices, and examining the behavior of $\hat{\alpha}$
in very high-dimensional settings where $n/p \ll 1$.

\section{Proof That $1 + \beta \geq 0$}
\label{app:proof}
It is clear from \eqref{new_OAS} that $\rho_{\text{OAS-Extended}} \leq 1$.
We show $1 + \beta \geq 0$, establishing the lower bound.
The argument is identical for the population quantity $\beta$ and the sample estimator
$\hat{\beta}$; we write $A$ for either $\Sigma$ or $\hat{S}$, and $V$ for either
$\operatorname{Var}(\lVert X \rVert^2)$ or $\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\lVert X \rVert^2)$.

\begin{proof}
Both variance quantities are non-negative: the population variance by definition, and
\[
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\lVert X \rVert^2)
  = \tfrac{1}{n}\sum_k \lVert X^k \rVert^4 - \operatorname{Tr}^2(\hat{S}) \geq 0
\]
by Jensen's inequality on the empirical distribution.
Since $\alpha = V - 2\operatorname{Tr}(A^2)$, we have $\alpha \geq -2\operatorname{Tr}(A^2)$.
Noting $\beta = \alpha(1-1/p)/M$, it suffices to show $M \geq 2(1-1/p)\operatorname{Tr}(A^2)$,
i.e.\ $\operatorname{Tr}^2(A) \geq \operatorname{Tr}(A^2)$.
For any positive semidefinite $A$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_p \geq 0$,
\[
\operatorname{Tr}^2(A) - \operatorname{Tr}(A^2)
= \Bigl(\sum_i \lambda_i\Bigr)^2 - \sum_i \lambda_i^2
= 2\sum_{i < j} \lambda_i \lambda_j \geq 0.
\]
Hence $1 + \beta \geq 0$, so $\rho_{\text{OAS-Extended}} \in [0,1]$ for both the
population cumulant and the sample estimator.
\end{proof}

\subsection*{Supplementary Note S1. Inter-LLM Agreement and the Consensus Gate}
\label{sec:interllm}

Because only diarrhea has an expert ground truth, we also measured the agreement
between the two independently prompted agents, which requires no labels. Cohen's
$\kappa$ between LLM~1 (clinical NLP expert) and LLM~2 (GI/neurology specialist)
was computed over the 60,530 note--phenotype instances that both models
classified (Figure~\ref{fig:agreement}A). Overall agreement was high
($\kappa=0.930$, raw agreement 96.6\%), and all 17 phenotypes reached
$\kappa\geq0.73$, with per-phenotype values in Table~\ref{tab:kappa_supp}. Seven
of the 60,537 matches did not return a valid YES or NO from both models and were
scored negative. Because the two prompts were written independently, their
agreement is a proxy for how well specified a phenotype is. It does not track the
per-phenotype expert agreement from the spot-check, however. Attention/alertness has
the lowest $\kappa$ (0.732) yet reached 6/6 on review, while dysautonomia
($\kappa=0.917$) and refusing medication ($\kappa=0.890$) reached only 4/6. With six
cases per phenotype the spot-check cannot resolve differences of that size, so the two
signals should be read as independent rather than concordant.

Diarrhea is scored by the diarrhea-specific pipeline rather than by the presence
prompt, and reaches $\kappa=0.878$ at raw agreement 98.0\% over the 2,260 notes both
agents classified. It is therefore shown separately from the 17, as a hatched bar in
Figure~\ref{fig:agreement}A and below the rule in Table~\ref{tab:kappa_supp}.

\paragraph{Prompt wording drives agreement.}
The two diarrhea prompts isolate what wording alone contributes, because both
were applied to the identical 2,260 notes with the same two models. The
deployed prompt~V0 reaches raw agreement 95.1\% and $\kappa=0.805$, and the
reported prompt~V2 reaches 98.0\% and $\kappa=0.878$
(Table~\ref{tab:llm_contingency}). Specifying the target more tightly leaves the
two agents less room to differ, and the same effect appears at the cell level
across the prompt ladder (Table~\ref{tab:prompt_variants}). Among the 17
phenotypes the two lowest values are attention/alertness ($\kappa=0.732$) and the
open-ended other-side-effects category ($0.756$), which are also the two whose
target is least concretely specifiable. Inter-LLM disagreement may therefore be a
useful label-free signal for which phenotypes most need prompt refinement or human
review, although the present spot-check is too small to validate it.

\paragraph{What the consensus gate costs and buys.}
Across the full corpus the two agents disagreed on 3.4\% of instances
(Figure~\ref{fig:agreement}B, with raw counts in
Table~\ref{tab:llm_contingency}). The gate resolves these disagreements
conservatively, counting only ``both~YES'' instances (38.4\%) as positive and
treating one-sided calls as negative. This is how it suppresses one-sided false
positives, at some cost in recall. On the diarrhea ground truth the mechanism is
measurable but small. Under the deployed prompt, the only configuration for which
both agents were also scored alone, the gate changes two of 183 cells against the
stronger of them (Table~\ref{tab:prompt_variants}, panel~A), so it neither costs
nor buys measurable accuracy there. The case for two agents rests on making their
disagreement observable across the 17 phenotypes that have no ground truth.

\paragraph{The voting pattern as a confidence signal.}
Partitioning cells by the two agents' votes shows that cells where both agree No
are the most accurate against the expert labels (84.3\%, 113/134), cells where
both agree Yes are the least accurate (52.3\%, 23/44), and split votes fall
between them (72.7\%, 8/11). The low accuracy of ``both~Yes'' cells is the
threshold-disagreement effect described in the main-text error analysis. The
agents confidently and defensibly detect documented diarrhea that the reviewer
scored as sub-threshold, so positive calls are exactly the cells a deployment
should route for human adjudication.

\paragraph{Why the reported configuration's run-to-run SD is zero.}
Prompt~V2's accuracy in main-text Table~2 carries an SD of 0.0 because its
confusion matrix is identical in all three runs, at 30~true positives,
124~true negatives, 12~false positives and 17~false negatives. This is a property
of the aggregation step and not evidence that the prompt is deterministic. At the
note level the consensus call does move, flipping on 7,~9 and~8 of the 2,260
classified notes across the three run pairs, and on 3,~4 and~3 of the 1,404
notes that fall inside the annotated patients' evaluation windows. None of those
flips changes a cell. Aggregation marks a patient--timepoint \emph{Yes} if
\emph{any} note in the six-month bucket receives a positive call, so a flip on a
note whose bucket already holds another positive is absorbed. The deployed
prompt~V0 flips on 15,~11 and~10 notes over the same pairs, and one of its cells
does move. The zero is therefore correct arithmetic at the cell level while the
underlying note-level classification remains stochastic, and it should not be
read as prompt stability.

\paragraph{Decoding parameters and the independence of the runs.}
No seed and no sampling parameters were set in any of the 42 model-invocation
nodes, so temperature, top-$p$, top-$k$ and the token limit took platform
defaults throughout, as the main-text Methods states. The three runs are
therefore independent draws rather than replays of a single run. We verified this
on the response strings themselves, since the platform exposes no per-call
telemetry. Under V2, Agent~1 returned byte-identical text on 2,243 of the
2,260 notes and Agent~2 on 2,251, whereas a cached or memoized path would
return identical strings everywhere. Byte differences outnumber label flips, so
part of the run-to-run variation is wording that leaves the YES/NO verdict
unchanged.


\subsection*{Supplementary Note S2. Model Development History}
\label{sec:model_history}

This note expands the model-development summary in the main-text Methods. The
pipeline was reached through a sequence of designs, each built to address a
failure mode observed in the previous one, and the benchmark of the six retained
methods against the 189-cell diarrhea ground truth is in
Table~\ref{tab:architecture}.

Two points bound how those numbers relate to the main text. First, the
architecture was selected on the original note corpus, the order-date exposure
anchor and a 189-cell grid, and it is reported here on the numbers it was decided
with. The architecture it settled on was then held fixed, and the prompt
comparison in the main text varies the prompt instead, on the refreshed corpus and
the corrected anchor. The two sets of numbers are not interchangeable. Second, the
\emph{negation-aware NLP} row of main-text Table~2 is not the \emph{rule-based
NLP} of Table~\ref{tab:architecture}. It is a reimplementation written for the
rerun so that every method in Table~2 is scored on one grid, and it reaches
42.1\% there against the 70.9\% of rule-based NLP. The \emph{regular expression} row
is the Stage~0 floor below, and matches its 42.3\% on the original grid.

\paragraph{Stage 0: Regex-only floor.}
The earliest approach flagged any note containing a diarrhea keyword. Recall is
high but precision is poor, because negated, historical, templated and
anticipatory mentions are all counted positive, as in ``denies diarrhea,'' ``had
diarrhea last year,'' checkbox review-of-systems fields and ``call if diarrhea
develops.'' Every subsequent design targets one of these false-positive sources.

\paragraph{Stage 1: Rule-based NLP.}
We added regular-expression negation detection and temporal cue matching to
discount past-tense and resolved mentions. This substantially improved precision
over the floor but was brittle. Hand-written patterns missed paraphrases and
complex sentence structure, and over-aggressive negation occasionally suppressed
true positives.

\paragraph{Stage 2: Hybrid NLP.}
We layered three further components onto the rule-based system. Clinical-form and
template filters remove boilerplate and blank-field matches, severity gates
down-weight ``mild,'' ``controlled'' and ``resolving'' language, and simple
cross-temporal handling was added. At equal overall accuracy to the rule-based model, this
recovered recall that the stricter negation rules had removed, so the two systems
sat at different points on the same precision--recall frontier rather than one
dominating the other.

\paragraph{Stage 3: Iterative single-LLM prototype.}
Before the full ground truth existed, we prototyped a three-pass LLM approach on a
32-patient subset to test whether contextual reasoning could move beyond the
rule-based frontier. It established feasibility but used a different evaluation
set with no paired ground truth, so it is not part of the six-method benchmark.

\paragraph{Stage 4: Single-LLM and the dual-LLM consensus gate.}
Once the full ground truth was available, we evaluated a single
clinical-NLP-expert LLM, whose accuracy (72.7\%) edged above the rule-based
frontier (70.9\%) although the difference was not resolved at 189 cells. Adding a
second, differently prompted domain-specialist model raised the question of how to
combine the two outputs. We tested both aggregation rules on identical model
outputs. An OR-gate (\emph{permissive}, positive if either agent says Yes)
maximizes sensitivity but readmits false positives, while an AND-gate
(\emph{consensus}, positive only if both agree) favors precision. The consensus
gate gave the best overall accuracy and the most run-stable operating point, and
was adopted.

\paragraph{Rejected variant: a broader definition of the target.}
Having fixed the gate, we tried loosening what the prompt counts as a positive.
Both agents were instructed to score any documented diarrhea as present,
dropping the exclusion for diarrhea that was mild or already controlled with
medication, on the reasoning that a symptom under treatment is still a symptom.
This raised recall as intended but added far more false positives than it
recovered true ones, so overall accuracy fell well below the adopted design and
the change was reverted. Note~S7 quantifies the same effect on the reported grid
as versions~V1 and~V4.

\paragraph{What the pairwise tests do and do not establish.}
Table~\ref{tab:architecture}, panel~B, reports all 15 pairwise McNemar exact tests
on the identical 189-cell paired ground truth. Every context-aware method
significantly outperforms the regex floor ($p<0.0001$, and after Holm correction).
The comparisons above the floor are directionally consistent with the accuracy
ordering, with the consensus model winning each head-to-head disagreement, for
example 24 discordant cells to 14 against hybrid NLP, but none reaches
significance ($p=0.11$--$1.0$). This reflects limited power rather than an absence
of effect. The consensus-versus-NLP gap rests on a net of roughly ten cells of
189, and confirming a difference of that size at 80\% power would require on the
order of 550 annotated cells, about three times the current ground truth. The
final rerun sharpens the same reading. On the refreshed corpus and the corrected
anchor the gate reaches 79.6\% and the stronger single agent 79.2\%, differing on
two of 183 cells (Table~\ref{tab:prompt_variants}, panel~A). We therefore adopt
the consensus gate as the best-performing configuration on present evidence, and
for the observability of the two agents' disagreement across the 17 phenotypes
that have no ground truth, rather than as a proven necessity.

\paragraph{Multi-phenotype run configuration.}
The 17-phenotype presence results in main-text Figure~3 and in
Tables~\ref{tab:kappa_supp}, \ref{tab:side_effects}, \ref{tab:improvements} and
\ref{tab:llm_contingency} were produced by the same model as the reported diarrhea
configuration. Both agents ran Claude~Opus~4.6 and issued 60,537 calls each, for
121,074 in total, with temperature, top-$p$, top-$k$, maximum tokens and seed all
left at platform defaults. The denominator for these percentages is the 99
patients whose exposure anchor could be confirmed, which is the 108 of Table~1 less
the 9 who have no reliable start date and therefore no windows to score. The two
paths assign notes to windows slightly differently. The multi-phenotype path
converts a day offset to months by dividing by 30.44 while the diarrhea grid uses
day bounds, which places 26,773 notes in window on the multi-phenotype side
against the 26,763 the diarrhea grid counts. We report the diarrhea grid figure
throughout, since that is the corpus the validated result rests on.

\paragraph{In-sample versus out-of-sample evidence.}
Architecture selection was informed by errors on the same 189 cells used to report
the architecture comparison, and prompt selection by errors on the same 183 cells
used to report the prompt comparison, so both diarrhea accuracies are in-sample
estimates and are upper bounds rather than held-out validations. The architecture, the
consensus gate and the prompt design were then frozen and carried to the remaining 17
phenotypes with only the phenotype definition substituted (Note~S3.4), and their
expert spot-check agreement in the main-text Results is the out-of-sample evidence
that the design transfers.

\subsection*{Supplementary Note S4. Reading the Error Taxonomy, and Intended Use}
\label{sec:extended_discussion}

\paragraph{How to read the error taxonomy.}
The taxonomy in main-text Table~4 covers the 29 errors of the reported
configuration. Two points about it are worth stating.

The taxonomy does not contain a category for the model misreading a note, and that
absence is a limit of the method rather than a finding. Each error was assigned by
rule, from where the supporting evidence sits relative to the scored window, so the
categories can separate a window-placement mismatch from a threshold disagreement
but cannot tell whether a note was misread within its own window. The prompts emit
only YES or NO, so nothing in the output records the reasoning behind a call.

The 91.8\% quoted in the main text is a bound and not a corrected accuracy. It is
what accuracy becomes if every threshold-disagreement cell is re-scored as correct
wherever the model and the note agree the symptom is present. Reaching it
defensibly would require re-adjudicating the ground truth prospectively, under a
severity threshold written into both the annotation guideline and the prompt,
rather than relabeling the current errors after the fact.

\paragraph{Intended use.}
The operating point we report, precision~0.714 and recall~0.638 on diarrhea, is
well suited to \emph{cohort-level} inference and triage but not to autonomous
per-patient decision-making. At this precision and recall the pipeline is best used
to estimate phenotype prevalence and trajectories across a population, where over-
and under-calls partially offset in aggregate, and to surface candidate notes for a
human reviewer. Errors are also non-random, concentrating in threshold-ambiguous
cases, so any per-patient use should keep a clinician in the loop and treat a
positive call as a prompt for review rather than a conclusion. We therefore frame
the extracted rates as a real-world evidence and hypothesis-generation tool, and
the individual note classifications as a triage aid.

\subsection*{Supplementary Note S6. Annotation Procedure}
\label{sec:annotation_guideline}

The diarrhea ground truth and the multi-phenotype expert spot-check were
established by the Rett Center clinical team, comprising two pediatric nurses
familiar with the Rett syndrome clinic and two pediatric neurologists, who worked
as a single reviewing group throughout. For each patient and timepoint window the
reviewers examined the available clinical notes and labeled the cell Yes for
medication-associated diarrhea, No, or Deceased/Not~applicable. Where diarrhea was
recorded, its severity was noted on the clinic's four-level scale: 1, loose stool in
diaper; 2, watery stool in diaper; 3, watery stool on clothes; 4, watery stool
outside clothes. The operative question was
whether documented diarrhea represented a medication side effect as opposed to a
tolerated, controlled or pre-existing baseline symptom. This is the same judgment
that drives the reviewer--model threshold disagreements in main-text Table~4.

The reviewers resolved each cell together by consensus rather than annotating
independently against a written guideline. No formal written guideline was issued,
and because each cell was adjudicated by consensus, no inter-annotator agreement
statistic could be computed retrospectively. This is a genuine limitation for
gold-standard reliability (TRIPOD-LLM items 8a--8c). A shared written guideline with
an explicit severity threshold, applied by independent double annotation, would both
tighten the ground truth and allow the reviewer--model threshold disagreements to be
quantified rather than adjudicated case by case.

\paragraph{Scope of the spot-check sample.}
The spot-check sample was drawn before the exposure-anchor adjudication was final,
so its coverage of the reported evaluation windows is partial. Of the 102 reviewed
notes, 58 fall inside an evaluation window in the reported configuration and 44 do
not. The shortfall is concentrated at baseline, where 26 of 33 cases fall outside,
against 12 of 34 at 6~months, 6 of 34 at 12~months and 0 of 1 at 18~months. That
gradient follows from the baseline window being the one defined immediately around
the anchor, so it is the most sensitive to where the anchor sits, while the later
windows are progressively less so. A failure of record linkage would instead have
removed cases uniformly. The shortfall is balanced with respect to the model's call,
affecting 22 of the 51 model-positive and 22 of the 51 model-negative cases, so the
58 are not tilted toward agreement or disagreement. On those 58 the reported
configuration returns the same call in 57 cases, and expert agreement over them is
91.4\% (53/58). The 90.2\% (92/102) in the main text is the figure the reviewers
produced over the notes they read, and we report it as such. Re-estimating agreement
directly on the reported configuration would require a fresh sample.

\subsection*{Supplementary Note S7. Prompt-Level and Variable-Decomposition
Sensitivity Analyses}

Note~S2 describes how the \emph{architecture} was selected. Holding that
architecture fixed, we ran three further experiments on the refreshed corpus and
the corrected exposure anchor to ask which component of the configuration the
remaining error is attributable to. The first varied the prompt wording, and it is
where the reported configuration comes from. The second replaced the single
extraction question with two simpler questions combined by an explicit rule. The
third left the extraction untouched and realigned each patient's sequence of
predictions in time. The main text carries the prompt comparison as Table~2, while
the realignment appears only here, because it presumes that onset falls at the
first on-treatment visit and is therefore a diagnostic of where the error sits
rather than a deployable comparator.

The version identifiers used in this supplement and in the released code
correspond to the main-text names as follows. V0 is \emph{uncontrolled diarrhea},
the deployed prompt; V1 is \emph{any diarrhea}; V2 is \emph{severe diarrhea}, the
reported prompt; V3 is \emph{severe diarrhea with rules}; V4 is \emph{any diarrhea
with rules}; and S1 is the \emph{onset-aligned} variant. \emph{Severe} denotes the
clinical-significance bar quoted verbatim in Note~S3, that the diarrhea be active
and either causing ongoing concern or prompting a change in management.
\emph{With rules} denotes the pair of rules that treat resolved diarrhea, and
diarrhea attributed to another cause, as absent.

\subsubsection*{Prompt wording}

Five prompt versions were compared on the same 183 annotated diarrhea cells, with
the two agents, the consensus gate, the keyword pre-filter and the output schema
all unchanged. Two elements were varied. The first is the severity threshold,
specifically whether diarrhea being controlled with medication counts as present.
The second is a pair of explicit reasoning rules stating that a resolution later in
a note governs an earlier onset, and that a finding attributed to another cause is
absent. Version~V0 is the deployed prompt and serves as the base case. Each version
was run three times. Table~\ref{tab:prompt_variants} reports the results, and three
findings follow.

First, \textbf{the severity threshold is the only element that moves accuracy}.
Restating the deployed exclusion explicitly and adding a severity bar raised
accuracy from 79.6\% to 84.2\% (V0 to V2), the largest movement anywhere in the
family. The mechanism is precision. False positives fall from 21 to 12 while true
positives are essentially unchanged at 31 and 30, so the added bar suppresses calls
on documented but managed diarrhea without giving up detections. The difference is
nonetheless not established, as it rests on 9 cells won against 1 lost, which is
$p=0.021$ before correction and $p=0.15$ after Holm correction across the seven
comparisons in this family.

Second, \textbf{the explicit reasoning rules add nothing}. V3, which is V2 plus
those rules, scores 83.1\% against V2's 84.2\%, differing on two cells of 183
($p=0.50$), and V0 to V3 changes 12 cells for a net of six ($p=0.35$ after
correction). The reason is that the deployed prompt already carried both
instructions in weaker form, stating that historical references where the finding
has clearly resolved are absent, and that findings attributed to another cause are
absent (Note~S3). The added rules therefore restated existing guidance rather than
supplying a new criterion. The residual temporal errors in main-text Table~4
reflect inconsistent application of a rule the prompt already contained, and
restating that rule more forcefully did not correct them.

Third, \textbf{reclassifying medication-controlled diarrhea as present made
performance worse}, by 4.4~points in V1 and 4.6~points in V4, consistently across
all three runs. The mechanism is a poor trade, adding 14~false positives to remove
6~false negatives. This is the same direction as the broader definition of the
target that was tested and reverted during development (Note~S2), now quantified on
the reported grid, and it is why the deployed prompt treats adequately controlled
diarrhea as absent. Neither broader
version is significantly worse than V0 on this grid ($p=0.35$ and $p=0.25$ after
correction), so the threshold choice is supported by a consistent direction across
runs and versions rather than by a resolved test.

Model count is not one of the elements that matters here. Running either agent
alone under V0 gives 78.5\% and 79.2\%, and the gate's 79.6\% differs from the
stronger single agent on two cells, so the whole spread in
Table~\ref{tab:prompt_variants} is attributable to wording rather than to the
number of calls (Note~S1).

The ranking also survives dropping the pre-treatment baseline. The 54 baseline cells
are almost all true negatives and inflate every configuration equally, and on the
129~on-treatment cells alone the deployed prompt scores 72.9\%, the reported prompt
79.1\% at precision 0.750, and the onset-aligned variant 79.1\% at recall 0.745.
Removing baseline therefore costs the reported configuration 5.1~points without
changing which configuration wins. These three are computed from the modal
predictions rather than as three-run means, because the per-timepoint confusion
counts were exported for the modal run only, which is also why the two rule-based
methods and versions~V1, V3 and~V4 cannot be shown this way.

\subsubsection*{Decomposing the extraction question}

The prompt experiment leaves open the possibility that the single extraction
question asks for two judgments at once, whether diarrhea has started and whether it
is currently uncontrolled. We tested that reading by replacing the single question
with two simpler ones and combining them in code rather than in the prompt.
Variable~A asks only whether diarrhea has begun as a side effect of trofinetide at
any point up to and including the visit. Variable~B asks only whether it is
adequately controlled at the visit. The two were combined by a deterministic state
rule that labels diarrhea present from the visit at which onset is first detected
and absent from the visit at which control is first established. Ten combination
rules were evaluated, varying that rule, the direction of the consensus gate and the
within-window aggregation order, all at no additional inference cost, since each is
a function of the same two extracted variables.

The decomposition did \textbf{not improve on the single question}. The ten rules
span 61.7\% to 79.4\% (Table~\ref{tab:prompt_variants}, panel~B), the best coming
within 0.2~points of the deployed prompt and none reaching the 84.2\% of the
reported configuration. The onset variable is what limits them. Applied alone it
scores 61.7\% at precision 0.384, so it fires on 61 of the 136~negative cells, and
because the state rule cannot label a visit negative until control is documented,
the combination rules can only recover accuracy by suppressing harder, which
collapses recall. As with the reasoning rules above, the deployed prompt already
encodes this logic, since it scores active diarrhea as present and both resolved
history and adequately controlled disease as absent (Note~S3). Splitting that
judgment into two questions and a state machine reproduced it less accurately than
asking it once.

\subsubsection*{Realigning the predictions in time}

Correcting the exposure anchor removes the dispensing and titration delay from the
window boundaries (Note~S8), but it cannot remove the lag between a symptom starting
and a note recording it. A third experiment asked what accuracy would be available
in the best case, if the anchor and the annotation agreed on when diarrhea began. We
left the extraction untouched and slid each patient's sequence of predicted visits so
that the first visit predicted positive falls at the first on-treatment visit, padding
the vacated tail as negative. Only the model output moves, so every cell remains
comparable against the same annotation. Applied to the deployed prompt's modal
predictions this raised accuracy from 79.8\% to 84.2\%, the best F1 anywhere in the
family at 0.707 (variant~S1 in Table~\ref{tab:prompt_variants}, panel~C), matching
the reported prompt from the opposite direction, by cutting false negatives rather
than false positives.

This is a bound and not a method. Collapsing every patient's onset to the first
on-treatment visit removes any possibility of predicting a later onset, so it assumes
away the case of a patient who develops the symptom after a year. For diarrhea that
assumption is nearly free, since the annotation places 35 of the 37 positive patients
at their first on-treatment visit, but it is not an assumption we could carry to the
other phenotypes, where onset is not concentrated at a single visit. A related
benchmark makes the same point about the task. Predicting from the visit number
alone, positive at 6~months and negative everywhere else, scores 82.5\% on these
cells, because 35 of the 47 positive cells sit at that one visit. Much of the
annotated signal is carried by the timing of the visit relative to treatment start
rather than by the content of the individual note, which is a property of this
label set rather than a result about the model.

\paragraph{How these experiments sit in the development process.}
The results above are the final stage of an iterative process and not a set of
independent replications. We first searched over architectures, then over prompts,
running rounds of error analysis between stages and carrying the surviving
configuration forward each time. Two things changed along the way. Error analysis
showed that some of the remaining error was in the data rather than in the model, so
the note pull was extended from one ending in 2025 to one extending through August
2026, and the exposure anchor was replaced (Note~S8). Earlier stages were therefore
run on a different corpus and a different set of evaluation windows, and their
numbers are not comparable to the ones reported here. Where an earlier stage and the
final run disagree, we report the final run.

Model builds differ between the two for the same reason. Every configuration of the
final rerun ran in one session on Claude~Opus~4.6~v1.154.0 and the arms are therefore
mutually comparable, while the architecture comparison in
Table~\ref{tab:architecture} ran on the build the pipeline was originally deployed
with, v1.151.0. The platform withdrew v1.151.0 before the rerun, so a byte-identical
replication of the deployed configuration was not available and the two sets are
reported separately rather than pooled.

\subsection*{Supplementary Note S8. The Exposure Anchor}

Every follow-up window is measured from the date trofinetide was started, so that
date determines which visit a note is scored against. The deployed pipeline took it
from the earliest trofinetide record in the Epic order table, and the resulting
windows disagreed with the expert annotation more often than the note content did.
Manual review of the record explained why. Trofinetide is an oral solution dispensed
by a specialty pharmacy and given at home, so the drug appears in orders, charts and
correspondence well before the family gives the first dose, and the order is followed
by pharmacy processing, insurance authorization and a four-week titration. In one
reviewed patient the prescription reached the specialty pharmacy 73~days after the
order, insurance declined coverage the same day, and the first record of the family
giving the drug is at day~114. In another the order preceded the first documented
dose by more than two years. In both cases the agents read every note correctly and
the error was in which window the note had been placed.

We therefore replaced the order date with the earliest documented \emph{exposure},
taken in order of preference from the medication administration record, then from a
dispense or fill record, and otherwise from the earliest note adjudicated as
documenting active dosing. Of the 108~QC-confirmed patients, 8 anchor on an
administration record and 91 on an adjudicated note, while 9 have no reliable
evidence of a start date and are excluded from the timepoint analysis. None anchors
on a dispense record, because trofinetide fills go through a specialty pharmacy and
never reach the institutional dispense tables. The correction is large and does not
depend on the labels, moving the median patient by 116~days, with more than half
moving by more than 90~days. It also moves six
cells out of the follow-up range, taking the grid from 189 cells to 183 while
conserving the contributing patients and the 47 positive cells, and accuracy under
the deployed prompt rises from 77.1\% to 79.6\%. That rise cannot be attributed to
the anchor alone, because the note corpus was refreshed in the same rerun, so we
report the two grids side by side. Two negative controls confirm that the result does
not follow from displacing windows as such, since neither randomly re-anchoring the
patients nor permuting their timepoint labels reaches the observed accuracy in 200
draws.

The corrected anchor does not remove the problem entirely. It cannot recover the lag
between a symptom starting and a note recording it, and the annotation is cell-level
and carries no dates, so a reviewer may place a symptom at the stage of treatment
where it clinically belongs rather than at the timestamp of the note that records it.
Both effects are visible in the gap between the two ways of scoring the pipeline.
Judged note by note, where the anchor plays no part, agreement with expert review is
about 90\%, at 90.2\% over the full 17-phenotype spot-check and 91.4\% over the 58
of those cases that fall inside an evaluation window (Note~S6). Judged cell by cell, where
every call must also land in the right six-month window, the reported configuration
reaches 84.2\%. We read the difference as the cost of identifying the start date from
the record rather than as a failure to read the notes, which is why the residual
temporal errors in main-text Table~4 are the largest remaining category after
threshold disagreement.

\begin{abstract}
In the best-arm identification problem, an algorithm adaptively selects arms to find the arm of the largest mean reward. Successive Rejects (SR) is a simple fixed-budget best-arm identification algorithm that eliminates one candidate arm at each phase.
At first glance, SR seems to have limited adaptivity, since it follows predetermined phase lengths. However, for Gaussian arms with common variance, SR's worst-instance error exponent normalized by the popular complexity measure $H_1(P)$ is optimal up to a constant factor, which partly explains why SR's performance is competitive compared with state-of-the-art adaptive sampling algorithms. In this paper, we extend the framework of SR by optimizing its predefined schedule of phase lengths.
We formulate phase-schedule design as an optimization problem for the normalized error exponent.
Then, we introduce a version of SR with the optimized schedule, which we call $H_1$-balanced Successive Rejects (\HSR{}).
This schedule is optimal within the class of SR-type algorithms with deterministic equal-count schedules.
For Gaussian arms with common variance, $H_1$-SR achieves at least $11/12$
of the optimal normalized rate over all adaptive algorithms for every
$K\ge2$, and this approximation ratio converges to one as
$1-O(1/\log K)$ as $K\to\infty$. This is a significant improvement over original SR,
whose corresponding fraction of the optimal normalized rate converges to $1/4$.
Finally, experiments on ten synthetic instances and two dataset-derived Gaussian
benchmarks compare the optimized schedule with original SR at finite
horizons. They show substantial gains on many instances while also
exposing a regime in which more aggressive early elimination is costly.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Best-arm identification asks how to use noisy measurements to select the
alternative with the largest mean. The forecaster, who follows an algorithm, adaptively chooses which
arm to measure and, after a prescribed budget of $T$ observations, outputs
a final recommendation: its estimate of the best arm. 

Successive Rejects (SR; \citealp{audibert2010best}) is a particularly simple
elimination algorithm that involves $K-1$ phases. Each phase gives the same number
of additional samples to every remaining arm, then eliminates the arm
with the smallest cumulative empirical mean. The phase lengths are fixed
in advance.
Sequential Halving (SH; \citealp{karnin2013almost}) uses a similar design
but eliminates approximately half the remaining arms in each phase.
These methods show that simple elimination can achieve an exponentially
small probability of error.
The multiplicative constant in the exponential rate, however,
determines how much budget is needed when small error probabilities matter.

The two methods also differ in how they use observations. Original SH
ranks arms using samples collected in the current phase, whereas SR
retains earlier samples in each surviving arm's empirical mean. This
distinction can affect finite-budget performance.
SR remains a competitive benchmark alongside more recent algorithms such as Continuous Rejects
\citep{wang2023large} and Almost Tracking \citep{komiyama2026anytime}.
Its continued relevance raises two questions: how close is its error
rate to the best attainable rate, and can a small change to its schedule
close the remaining gap?

The limited adaptivity of SR makes its performance gap particularly intriguing.
Once the rejection rule is fixed---sample all surviving arms equally and
eliminate an arm with the smallest cumulative empirical mean---the
only remaining design choice is the \emph{clock}: how many observations should each surviving arm have when each elimination takes
place. 
Original SR makes one particular choice. 
It is not immediate whether that choice is well matched to the statistical difficulty of
avoiding an erroneous elimination.

We therefore study the phase schedule itself as an optimization variable.
Our argument proceeds from the outside in. We first place an information
bound on the $H_1$-normalized rate of an arbitrary adaptive algorithm, where the $H_1$ is a popularly used complexity measure of the instance.
We then
restrict attention to the class of SR-type algorithms with deterministic equal-count
schedules, which is a subset of all adaptive algorithms that includes the original SR, and ask for the best schedule in that class. A sharp analysis of the event that the true best arm is simultaneously below all surviving
competitors turns the statistical problem into a small deterministic
balancing problem. Solving it produces the phase schedule; the algorithm
is a consequence of that optimization. 

\subsection{How should we compare identification algorithms?}

An algorithm can work well when one arm is clearly better and struggle
when several arms have nearly equal means. Comparing raw error
probabilities across such instances confounds algorithm quality with
problem difficulty. We therefore account for the gaps between arm means
before comparing how quickly errors decrease with the budget.
Following \citet{komiyama2022minimax,komiyama2026anytime}, we compare
the worst-instance exponential rate after normalization by an instance
complexity. We use $H_1$, the sum of inverse squared gaps to the best
arm, as a complexity measure that we normalize the error rate. 
A larger normalized rate means a stronger guarantee relative to
this measure of difficulty. 

Our benchmark is the best such rate over \emph{all} adaptive algorithms, not just elimination methods. The algorithm does not know the true gaps;
$H_1$ is used to evaluate it, not as an input. This criterion does not 
require matching a gap-informed oracle on every instance
\citep{degenne2023existence}. We give the formal definition in
Section~\ref{sec:model}.

Our algorithm can be used to the best-arm identification with sub-Gaussian rewards, including rewards supported in $[0,1]$ (or any finite region). 
Our optimality is for Gaussian rewards as we provides the error rate lower bound to that case. 

\subsection{Contributions}

The contributions follow the same progression as the analysis.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{An explicit characterization of the best rate for any adaptive algorithm.} For Gaussian arms we derive an explicit upper bound $R_K^\star\le 1/(\sigma^2B_K)$ on the best
$H_1$-normalized rate attainable by arbitrary adaptive algorithms.
\item \textbf{Optimization within the class of SR-type algorithms.}
We characterize the worst-instance rate of deterministic equal-count successive-rejection schedules. Its unique solution gives us \HSR{} algorithm, that achieves the matching rate.
\item \textbf{Comparison with all algorithms and with original SR.} The
optimized schedule satisfies $R_{\HSR}/R_K^\star\ge B_K/D_K\ge11/12$ for
every $K$, with $B_K/D_K=1-O(1/\log K)$, whereas original SR satisfies $R_{\mathrm{SR}}/R_K^\star\to1/4$ as $K\to\infty$.
Figure \ref{fig:phases} illustrates the difference between SR and \HSR{} in terms of budget allocation across phases.
\item \textbf{Finite-budget experiments.} On ten synthetic and two
dataset-derived Gaussian benchmarks we compare $H_1$-SR with original SR.
The experiments show that $\HSR{}$ often improves terminal error, while a deliberately highlighted failure case shows why the asymptotic worst-instance guarantee should not be read as pointwise finite-budget dominance.
\end{itemize}
