\subsection{Related work}\label{subsec_related}

\paragraph{Elimination algorithms}
Beyond SR \citep{audibert2010best} and Sequential Halving \citep{karnin2013almost,DBLP:conf/icml/ZhaoSSJ23}, \citet{shahrampour2017sequential} study
general sequential-elimination schedules, including nonlinear cumulative phase lengths. However, they have not characterized the optimal scheduling of the phase lengths.
\citet{wang2023large} develop a large-deviation analysis of
adaptive identification and introduce Continuous Rejects, which dynamically chooses the phase lengths.
\citet{barrier2023nonparametric} consider fixed-budget identification problems for a class of reward distributions bounded on $[0,1]$ and consider the SR algorithm therein.

\paragraph{Minimax rates and implementable algorithms.}
\citet{audibert2010best,carpentier2016tight} show that there is an $O(\log K)$ gap in the complexity of identifying the best arm between the fixed-budget setting (considered in this paper) and fixed-confidence settings, in which the algorithm can choose when to stop sampling.
A notable difference that subsequent research disclosed is that optimization in these two settings is fundamentally different.
Namely, the fixed-confidence setting allows a uniformly good algorithm. Namely, there exist several algorithms such as Track and Stop \citep{garivier2016optimal} and Top-two Thompson Sampling \citep{Russo2020,jourdan2023varepsilon,DBLP:conf/nips/Bandyopadhyay0A24} that achieve this property, meaning they perform optimally on all problem instances, whereas in the fixed-budget setting, no such uniformly good algorithm exists \citep{komiyama2022minimax,wang2023large,degenne2023existence,DBLP:conf/icml/WangAP24}. Therefore, the latter setting is closer to traditional statistical decision theory\footnote{Note that, in the statistical decision theory framework, it is usually called the risk measure.} \citep{Jenninson1982}, where the optimality depends on the choice of the complexity measure $H(P)$, such as admissibility \citep{imbens2025admissibility} and minimax optimality \citep{komiyama2022minimax}.
In particular, \citet{komiyama2022minimax} formulate minimax rates given a complexity measure $H(P)$, and introduce the delayed optimal tracking (DOT) algorithm. However, DOT is almost impossible to implement in practice as it needs to solve a dynamic program with a long horizon.
Later on, \cite{komiyama2026anytime} proposed a practical algorithm called simple tracking that does not require the information on the horizon $T$, and its version called almost tracking, which has a provable constant-factor rate guarantee. However, its constant on top of the rate guarantee is impractically large.

Our main results start from a more practical viewpoint. Starting from the popularly used SR algorithm, we improve its performance without introducing additional complexity into the algorithm.
Our main algorithm, \HSR{}, significantly improves the practical performance of SR, and we derive nearly minimax rate guarantees for the most popularly used complexity measure $H_1(P)$.

\section{From arbitrary adaptive algorithms to an optimized rejection schedule}
\label{sec:theory}

\subsection{Model and performance criterion}
\label{sec:model}

We follow the notation of \citet{komiyama2026anytime}. There are $K\ge2$
arms with unknown means $\bmP=(P_1,\ldots,P_K)$. At round $t$, algorithm
$\mathcal A$ chooses $I(t)\in[K]$ from the history up to round $t-1$,
then observes a fresh reward $X(t)$ from that arm. Write
\begin{equation}
 N_i(t)=\sum_{u=1}^t\ind\{I(u)=i\},\qquad
 Q_i(t)=\frac{\sum_{u=1}^t X(u)\ind\{I(u)=i\}}{N_i(t)}
 \quad(N_i(t)>0).
 \label{eq:observations}
\end{equation}
Thus $P_i$ is a true mean and $Q_i(t)$ is an empirical mean; write
$\bmQ(t)=(Q_1(t),\ldots,Q_K(t))$ once all arms have been sampled.
After the known horizon $T$, the algorithm recommends $J(T)$.

Assume a unique best arm and define
\[
 i^\star=i^\star(\bmP)=\argmax_{i\in[K]}P_i,\qquad
 P^\star=\max_iP_i,\qquad
 \Delta_i=P^\star-P_i>0\quad(i\ne i^\star).
\]
Parenthesized subscripts denote true ranks:
$P_{(1)}>P_{(2)}\ge\cdots\ge P_{(K)}$.
The unique-best assumption makes the target recommendation unambiguous
and ensures that every suboptimal gap is strictly positive.
For the exact-rate and minimax analysis, observations from arm $i$ are
independent draws from $N(P_i,\sigma^2)$, with a common variance
$\sigma^2>0$, and the reward streams are independent across arms.

We evaluate an algorithm through four quantities:

\begin{align}
 \PoE_{\mathcal A}(\bmP)&=\Prob_{\bmP}^{\mathcal A}
                  (J(T)\ne i^\star(\bmP)),&
 \Hone(\bmP)&=\sum_{i\ne i^\star(\bmP)}\Delta_i^{-2},\nonumber\\
 E_{\mathcal A}(\bmP)&=\liminf_{T\to\infty}
                  \frac1T\log\frac1{\PoE_{\mathcal A}(\bmP)},&
 R_{\mathcal A}&=\inf_{\bmP:\,\text{unique best}}
                  \Hone(\bmP)E_{\mathcal A}(\bmP).
 \label{eq:rate}
\end{align}
Here $\PoE_{\mathcal A}(\bmP)$ is the probability of recommending a
suboptimal arm after $T$ observations; as in
\citet{komiyama2022minimax}, its dependence on $T$ is implicit.
The complexity $H_1(\bmP)$ increases when competitors approach the best
arm, reflecting the greater difficulty of distinguishing their means.
The exponent $E_{\mathcal A}(\bmP)$ measures the asymptotic decrease of
error with budget: when a rate limit exists, the error behaves as
$\exp\{-T E_{\mathcal A}(\bmP)+o(T)\}$.
Finally, $R_{\mathcal A}$ is the smallest $H_1$-normalized exponent over
all unique-best instances. It measures the algorithm's worst-instance
guarantee after accounting for this complexity.

Let $\mathfrak A_K$ denote the class of all adaptive algorithm families
in this model, including randomized and horizon-dependent ones.
For each horizon $T$, arm selections may depend on the past observations
and internal randomness, and the final recommendation may depend on the
full observed history and internal randomness. These rules may depend
on $K$ and $T$, but not on the unknown means.
Our ideal objective is to attain the $H_1$-minimax rate
$R_K^\star=\sup_{\mathcal A\in\mathfrak A_K}R_{\mathcal A}$, or to guarantee a large
fraction of it with a practical algorithm. We determine SR's
normalized rate and improve it by changing only its phase lengths.

We exclusively consider $H_1$ here. Appendix~\ref{app:normalization} relates this convention to the other complexities studied in the literature \citep{audibert2010best,garivier2016optimal,komiyama2022minimax}.

For the finite-budget upper bound, we also allow independent rewards
with a common sub-Gaussian variance proxy $\sigma^2$: every centered
reward has moment generating function at most $e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}$
for all $\lambda\in\R$. 
In particular, our algorithm also has error rate guarantees under any rewards supported in $[0,1]$ by setting $\sigma^2=1/4$ in the analysis.
For these extensions, the error probability depends on the full reward laws, and could be the case that we can further improve the bounds when we have additional knowledge about the reward distributions.

\subsection{An information bound for every adaptive algorithm}
\label{sec:all-algorithm}

We first describe the possible achievable rates for any adaptive algorithm, including not only SR-type algorithms,
but also Continuous Rejects \citep{wang2023large} and Simple Tracking \citep{komiyama2026anytime}. 
Namely, let
\[
 h_m=\sum_{j=1}^m j^{-1},\qquad
 B_K=\begin{cases}
 8,&K=2,\\
 43/7+2h_{K-1},&K\ge3.
 \end{cases}
\]
The constant $B_K$ is an inverse-rate information constraint.

\begin{theorem}[Rate upper bound]\label{thm:converse}
For Gaussian arms and the criterion in \eqref{eq:rate},
$R_K^\star\le 1/(\sigma^2 B_K)$.
\end{theorem}

The proof is deferred to Appendix~\ref{app:converse}, which gives the full
change-of-measure argument and derives the explicit constant $B_K$ from a
single limiting allocation constrained by a hierarchy of Gaussian alternatives.
The theorem is a worst-instance asymptotic restriction; it is not a
finite-budget lower bound for every individual instance.

\subsection{The class of SR-type algorithms}\label{sec:srclass}

We now focus on the class of SR-type algorithms.
We consider all deterministic schedules (ie., the phase lengths are fixed in advance) and we preserve SR's sampling and rejection rules. 
Let $\mathfrak A_K^{\mathrm{SR}}\subseteq\mathfrak A_K$ be the class of SR-type
algorithms that sample every surviving arm to the same predetermined
cumulative count, reject one arm with a smallest empirical mean, and
recommend the last survivor. With $s$ arms remaining, denote the
cumulative count by $m_s(T)$. The counts are positive integers satisfying
\[
 m_K(T)\le\cdots\le m_2(T),\qquad
 2m_2(T)+\sum_{s=3}^K m_s(T)\le T.
\]
The budget counts each rejected arm at its final sample count and both
finalists at $m_2(T)$. Tie breaking in elimination is fixed. 

In summary, an algorithm in $\mathfrak A_K^{\mathrm{SR}}$ is characterized by the choice of the deterministic schedule $(m_K(T),\ldots,m_2(T))$. For example, as we discussed in Section~\ref{sec:srclass}, the original version of SR \citep{audibert2010best} corresponds to $m_s/T \propto 1/s$. We next relate the deterministic schedule to the algorithm's performance (i.e., error rate $R_{\mathcal A}$).

The rest of this section shows how the deterministic schedule $(m_K(T),\ldots,m_2(T))$ can be optimized. 

\subsection{How the deterministic schedule controls performance}\label{sec:geometry}

Consider a phase with $s$ surviving arms, while the true best arm is
still active. Rejecting it requires its empirical mean to be no larger
than those of all $s-1$ competitors at once. To analyze this event
without conditioning on survival, fix a deterministic candidate set $A=\{i^\star,i_1,\ldots,i_{s-1}\}$ containing the true best.
Define its true gaps and complexity by
\[
 \delta_j=P_{i^\star}-P_{i_j}>0,\qquad
 H_A=\sum_{j=1}^{s-1}\delta_j^{-2},
\]
that is, $\delta_j = \Delta_{i_j}$.
For the proof, let $\overline Q_{i,m}$ be the mean of the first $m$
rewards in arm $i$'s potential independent sequence. This is an
equivalent way to construct the sequential observations, not an extra
observation available to the algorithm. At any deterministic common count $m$, the empirical means of the arms in $A$ are represented by $\overline Q_{i,m}$.

We now relate the deterministic schedule to the SR-type algorithm's error exponent
through concentration inequalities. 
Namely, for Gaussian rewards with variance $\sigma^2$, the probability
that an arm's empirical mean falls below a fixed threshold
$q<P_i$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \Prob\!\left(\overline Q_{i,m}\le q\right)
 \le \exp\!\left(
 -m\KL\!\left(N(q,\sigma^2)\,\|\,N(P_i,\sigma^2)\right)
 \right)
 = \exp\!\left(-\frac{m(q-P_i)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).
 \label{eq:largedeviation}
\end{equation}


After subtracting $P^\star$, the true mean vector on $A$ is
$p_A=(0,-\delta_1,\ldots,-\delta_{s-1})$.
A necessary condition for rejecting the best arm is that the shifted
empirical vector belongs to
$\mathcal C_A=\{q\in\R^s:q_0\le q_j,\ 1\le j<s\}$.
This is a closed convex polyhedral cone, the intersection of the
half-spaces $q_0-q_j\le0$. It contains exactly the vectors in which the
true best arm has a smallest empirical mean, allowing ties. 
The quantity $d_A$ is the smallest Euclidean displacement of the
\emph{whole mean vector} that makes the true best arm empirically worst:
\begin{equation}
 d_A^2=\inf_{q\in\mathcal C_A}\|q-p_A\|^2
 =\min_{u\ge0}\left\{u^2+
             \sum_{j=1}^{s-1}(\delta_j-u)_+^2\right\}
 \ge\frac{(s-1)^2}{sH_A}.
 \label{eq:geometry}
\end{equation}
Here $(x)_+=\max\{x,0\}$ and $u$ is the downward displacement of
the best-arm empirical mean from $0$ to $-u$. For this fixed coordinate,
the nearest feasible competitor mean is $\max\{-\delta_j,-u\}$,
requiring an upward displacement $(\delta_j-u)_+$. Summing these squared
displacements and minimizing over $u$ gives the middle expression.
The inequality is tight when the gaps in $A$ are equal. Projection onto
this cone and a sub-Gaussian Chernoff bound, which gives a finite-sample
guarantee with the same quadratic structure in the exponent as
\eqref{eq:largedeviation}, give
\begin{equation}
 \Prob\!\left(\overline Q_{i^\star,m}\le
       \overline Q_{i,m}\ \text{for every }i\in A\setminus\{i^\star\}\right)
 \le \exp\left(-\frac{m(s-1)^2}{2s\sigma^2 H_A}\right).
 \label{eq:joint}
\end{equation}
Appendix~\ref{app:gaussian} proves both the projection step and the sharp
inverse-gap inequality. 
The large-deviation analysis of SR in
\citep{wang2023large,komiyama2026anytime} identifies the cost of such
misleading empirical means. Here we bound that cost, at the end of a phase $K+1-s$ where $s$ arms remains, sharply in terms of
$H_A$. Since $H_A \le H_1$, \eqref{eq:joint} also yields an upper bound in terms of $H_1$ that is uniform over all such sets $A$.
The analysis is enabled by the fact that an SR-type algorithm conducts uniform exploration at each phase, which is much more simpler than the design of algorithms appearing in \citep{wang2023large,komiyama2026anytime}.

The bound \eqref{eq:joint} is the key design input. Its coefficient depends only on the number $s$ of surviving arms. The next subsection packages this coefficient into a convenient quantity and asks how to choose all checkpoint counts so that no active-set size becomes the bottleneck.

\subsection{A small balancing problem with an explicit solution}\label{sec:balance}

The simultaneous-rejection bound in Section~\ref{sec:geometry} identifies
\[
 a_s=\frac{2s}{(s-1)^2},\qquad 2\le s\le K,
\]
as the information requirement associated with the checkpoint having $s$
surviving arms. Recall that $m_s(T)$ is the cumulative count per surviving arm
at the checkpoint with $s$ arms. 
An SR-type algorithm is characterized by $(m_s(T))_{2\le s\le K}$. Since this is a vector sequence of $T$, we take the limit as $T\to\infty$.
When the limits exist,
\[
 q_s=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{m_s(T)}{T},\qquad 2\le s\le K.
\]
Thus $q_s$ is a cumulative per-arm fraction, not the fraction spent in
that phase. 
For schedules without full limits,\footnote{Of course, such cases, for example, $m_s(T)$ quickly switches for different $T$, do not improve the rate!} Appendix~\ref{app:class} uses the same notation for limits along a common subsequence.
Since the error exponent is determined by the worst phase, the guaranteed normalized exponent is $\min_s q_s/(\sigma^2a_s)$.
Maximizing this among the class of limit fractions $(q_2,\ldots,q_K)$ gives
\begin{equation}
 \max_{\substack{0\le q_K\le\cdots\le q_2\\
                 2q_2+\sum_{s=3}^Kq_s\le1}}
       \min_{2\le s\le K}\frac{q_s}{a_s}.
 \label{eq:balance}
\end{equation}
Define the normalizing constant
\begin{equation}
 D_K:=2a_2+\sum_{s=3}^K a_s
 =4+2h_{K-1}+2h_{K-1}^{(2)},\qquad
 h_m^{(2)}=\sum_{j=1}^m j^{-2}.
 \label{eq:constants}
\end{equation}
The optimal limit fractions are given by $q_s$ such that \eqref{eq:balance} holds, is achieved by the following:
\begin{proposition}[Information balancing]\label{prop:balance}
The value of \eqref{eq:balance} is $1/D_K$, and its unique optimizer is
$q_s=a_s/D_K$ for all $s$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If the minimum is at least $v$, every $q_s\ge va_s$. The budget gives
$1\ge v(2a_2+\sum_{s=3}^Ka_s)=vD_K$. Equality is feasible because
$a_s$ decreases with $s$, and equality in the budget forces equality
in every coordinate lower bound.
\end{proof}


\subsection{The resulting algorithm and its guarantee}\label{sec:algorithm}

Proposition~\ref{prop:balance} determines the asymptotically balanced checkpoint fractions. We implement those fractions at finite horizon by integer rounding. For $T\ge K$, let $A_1=[K]$ and $n_0=0$. In phase
$k\in\{1,\ldots,K-1\}$, the active set has size $s=K+1-k$. Set
\begin{equation}
 n_k=1+\left\lfloor\frac{T-K}{D_K}\,a_{K+1-k}\right\rfloor.
 \label{eq:clock}
\end{equation}
The checkpoint $n_k$ is the cumulative sample count \emph{per surviving
arm}, not the global time. Each arm in $A_k$ receives $n_k-n_{k-1}$
additional samples. At the resulting global round $t_k$, all active
arms satisfy $N_i(t_k)=n_k$, and an arm minimizing the empirical mean $Q_i(t_k)$ is
removed. The phase therefore uses $(K+1-k)(n_k-n_{k-1})$ pulls.
Algorithm~\ref{alg:hsr} summarizes the procedure.

The following algorithm bounds the probability of error for Algorithm~\ref{alg:hsr}.
\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{$H_1$-balanced Successive Rejects (\HSR)}
\label{alg:hsr}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require Number of arms $K\ge2$; horizon $T\ge K$; fixed tie-breaking order
\State $A_1\gets[K]$, $n_0\gets0$; compute $D_K$ from \eqref{eq:constants}
\For{$k=1,\ldots,K-1$}
  \State $s\gets K+1-k$; $n_k\gets1+\lfloor(T-K)a_s/D_K\rfloor$
  \State Pull each $i\in A_k$ exactly $n_k-n_{k-1}$ additional times
  \State Let $t_k$ be the current round; $j_k\gets\argmin_{i\in A_k}Q_i(t_k)$
  \State $A_{k+1}\gets A_k\setminus\{j_k\}$
\EndFor
\State Set $J(T)$ to the unique element of $A_K$
\State If fewer than $T$ pulls were used, pad the budget and ignore those observations
\State \Return $J(T)$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\begin{theorem}[Finite-budget error upper bound]\label{thm:balanced}
For every $T\ge K$ and every unique-best instance with independent
$\sigma^2$-sub-Gaussian arm rewards,
\begin{equation}
 \PoE_{\HSR}(\bmP)\le
 \min\left\{1,(2^{K-1}-1)
 \exp\left(-\frac{T-K}{\sigma^2D_K\Hone(\bmP)}\right)\right\}.
 \label{eq:finite}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
Consequently, at every fixed instance the error exponent is at least
$1/(\sigma^2D_KH_1(\bmP))$. This gives
$R_{\HSR}\ge1/(\sigma^2D_K)$. 

In the Gaussian model, the asymptotic rate guarantee is tight:
Theorem~\ref{thm:class} below provides the matching upper bound,
yielding $R_{\HSR}=1/(\sigma^2D_K)$.

\subsection{Class optimality and comparison with any algorithm}\label{sec:classopt}

Since \HSR{} is designed to optimize the allocation of pulls across arms in a successive rejects framework, it achieves the best possible error exponent within this class of algorithms.
\begin{theorem}[Optimal clock within the class of SR-type algorithms]\label{thm:class}
For Gaussian arms,
$\sup_{\mathcal A\in\mathfrak A_K^{\mathrm{SR}}}R_{\mathcal A}=1/(\sigma^2D_K)$,
attained by \HSR.
\end{theorem}

The upper bound is enforced by a different hard instance at each
checkpoint. Consider $s$ arms with small gaps and $K-s$ arms with much
lower means. With high probability the latter are removed first, leaving
the difficult comparison to the $s$-arm checkpoint. Too few samples at
that checkpoint make best-arm rejection too likely. Applying this
argument to every $s$ yields simultaneous lower requirements on the
counts; their sum exhausts the budget at the proposed schedule.
Appendix~\ref{app:class} makes this argument precise.

This theorem identifies the best rate within $\mathfrak A_K^{\mathrm{SR}}$. Combining
it with the bound for arbitrary adaptive algorithms gives a separate
comparison with the unrestricted optimum.

\begin{corollary}[Uniform approximation and leading constant]\label{cor:factor}
For Gaussian arms and every fixed $K\ge2$,
\begin{equation}
 \frac{1}{\sigma^2D_K}\le R_K^\star\le\frac{1}{\sigma^2B_K},
 \qquad
 \frac{R_{\HSR}}{R_K^\star}\ge\frac{B_K}{D_K}
 \ge\frac{11}{12}.
 \label{eq:ratio}
\end{equation}
Moreover $B_K/D_K=1-O(1/\log K)$. As $K\to\infty$ after the
fixed-$K$ horizon limit, $R_{\HSR}/R_K^\star\to1$ and
$R_K^\star\sim1/(2\sigma^2\log K)$.
\end{corollary}
Corollary \ref{cor:factor} shows that \HSR{} is very close to the optimal rate attainable by any algorithm, which is somewhat surprising given the fact that it determines the length of the schedule beforehand and does not revisit the arms once they are eliminated.


\section{$H_1$-SR versus original Successive Rejects}\label{sec:srcompare}


\subsection{Sharp normalized-rate comparison}

For $T>K$, original SR uses
\begin{equation}
 n_k^{\mathrm{SR}}=
 \left\lceil\frac{T-K}{\barlog(K)(K+1-k)}\right\rceil,
 \qquad \barlog(K)=\frac12+\sum_{i=2}^K\frac1i.
 \label{eq:srclock}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp normalized original-SR comparison]\label{thm:sr}
For Gaussian arms under \eqref{eq:rate},
$R_{\mathrm{SR}}=1/(8\sigma^2\barlog(K))$.
For $T>K$,
\[
 \PoE_{\mathrm{SR}}(\bmP)\le
 \min\left\{1,\frac{K(K-1)}{4}
       \exp\left(-\frac{T-K}{8\sigma^2\barlog(K)\Hone(\bmP)}\right)\right\}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \frac{R_{\mathrm{SR}}}{R_K^\star}
 \ge\frac{B_K}{8\barlog(K)}\ge\frac14.
\]
\begin{equation}
 \frac{R_{\HSR}}{R_{\mathrm{SR}}}
     =\frac{8\barlog(K)}{D_K}\longrightarrow4,
 \qquad
 \frac{R_{\mathrm{SR}}}{R_K^\star}\longrightarrow\frac14.
 \label{eq:srgain}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
Theorem \ref{thm:sr} shows that, for $K\ge3$, \HSR{} achieves a strictly better worst-instance normalized exponent compared to the original SR algorithm, and it is by $4$ for large $K$.

For general $\sigma^2$-sub-Gaussian arms, the displayed finite-budget
bound remains valid with prefactor $K(K-1)/2$ instead of $K(K-1)/4$.
The smaller Gaussian prefactor uses an additional one-half tail factor;
the exact-rate and minimax comparisons in the theorem are Gaussian.

The exact error exponent of original SR is established in prior work \citep{DBLP:conf/icml/WangAP24,komiyama2026anytime}. 
Appendix~\ref{app:sr} gives the short
self-contained argument needed for the $H_1$ normalization used here.

\subsection{Intuition on the ratio}

Recall that $m_s(T)$ is the cumulative number of samples per
surviving arm at the phase with $s$ arms remaining.
Ignoring integer rounding, the two schedules satisfy
\[
\text{Original SR:}\quad
m_s(T)\approx\frac{T}{s\barlog(K)},
\qquad
\text{\HSR{}:}\quad
m_s(T)\approx\frac{T}{D_K}\frac{2s}{(s-1)^2}.
\]
Their ratio is therefore
\[
\frac{m_s^{\HSR}(T)}{m_s^{\mathrm{SR}}(T)}
\longrightarrow
\frac{2\barlog(K)}{D_K}
\left(\frac{s}{s-1}\right)^2
\qquad (T\to\infty).
\]
The ratio increases as fewer arms remain: $H_1$-SR spends less before early
eliminations and more on the final comparisons (Figure~\ref{fig:phases}). Since
$2\barlog(K)/D_K\to1$, the final-two ratio tends to $4$, matching the
large-$K$ rate improvement in Theorem~\ref{thm:sr}.

Optimizing the deterministic SR checkpoints yields $H_1$-SR, which is optimal
within this class of SR-type algorithms and achieves at least $11/12$ of the optimal Gaussian

to one as $K$ grows; original SR approaches $1/4$. Experiments show substantial
finite-budget gains on many instances but also a clear non-dominance case. The
finite-budget bound extends to independent sub-Gaussian rewards; matching
optimality beyond the Gaussian setting and the early/late elimination tradeoff
remain open.

\title{Sharp and Stable Label-Free Calibration Certificates from Logical Coherence}

\author{\name Takahiro Kato \email author@example.org \\

\begin{abstract}%
Query-conditioned probabilistic predictors, such as typed decision models, zero-shot classifiers and
the answer probabilities of language models, answer logically related questions one at a time. Their
answers need not be coherent, and the labels needed to check their calibration are often missing. We
ask what the law of the answers and their logical structure, without any label, can refute about
calibration. For every restriction on the information that a bettor's stakes may use, an
information-restricted minimax theorem identifies, for finitely supported laws of the answers, the
sharp label-free lower bound on the corresponding calibration residual: the largest bound that the
law of the answers and the logical structure allow. The theorem contains measures of incoherence,
feasible joint posteriors and the mutual calibration of forecasters as special cases. On bundles of
different, logically related events its mean, marginal and joint stages can separate strictly, and a
bound on a bundle cannot be attributed to a given one of its questions without assumptions on the
others. The sharp bound on marginal calibration error is discontinuous in the answers, the jump
needs logical constraints among the questions, and no label-free lower bound that is continuous in
the Wasserstein distance between laws of answers stays within a constant factor of it. Restricting
the stakes to Lipschitz functions gives a stable bound that is sharp for a smooth calibration
residual and, for every positive Lipschitz constant, is positive exactly when the sharp marginal
bound is. On an i.i.d.\ stream of bundles, stakes represented at fixed nodes and learnt by projected
online gradient ascent make it computable, with fixed-horizon certificates whose shortfall is
bounded by grid, learning and statistical terms, and predictable betting gives anytime-valid ones.
In a preregistered study of four predictors on two data sets, all seven confirmatory certificates
were positive (the eighth pair did not pass the pilot). A certificate shows only that calibration is
at least this bad; a certificate of zero means ``not refuted''.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keywords}
  calibration, label-free evaluation, probabilistic coherence, partial identification, Dutch books,
  anytime-valid inference
\end{keywords}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

A query-conditioned probabilistic predictor takes an input together with a question posed at
inference time and returns a probability. Typed decision models, which return a probability or a
distribution over named options instead of text, work this way, and so do zero-shot classifiers
built on a natural language inference (NLI) model and readouts of the answer probabilities of a
language model. Such a predictor is used by putting many small questions to one input and combining
the answers in code: a ticket goes to billing when the probability that it asks for a refund exceeds
a threshold, and to first-line support when the probability that it asks for something else does.
Each question is evaluated separately, so nothing forces the answers to logically related questions
to be the probabilities of a single probability measure, and audits that use no labels find that
they are not. On Jev, a commercial typed decision model that we also audit in
Section~\ref{sec:experiments}, the probabilities of ``the label is $X$'' and ``the label is not
$X$'' sum to a value that differs from one by $0.064$ on average, about five times the noise of
repeated calls, and the probabilities of three mutually exclusive labels, asked one at a time, sum
to $1.14$ on average \citep{li2026beyond}; when the same decision is broken into broad categories
and finer labels, the two disagree by a mean total variation of $0.219$ to $0.349$ on three data
sets \citep{joy2026system}. The model's documentation calls it calibrated. For the version we audit,
it also showed a question and its negation, asked separately, whose probabilities summed to $1.19$,
and a question that received $0.22$ when asked for one probability and $0.01$ for the option ``yes''
when asked as a choice between yes and no, and it advised not to hold the model to arithmetic
identities between separate questions; a later revision removed these examples
\citep{typesafe2026jaggedness}.

Routing rules such as the one above mean what they say only if the answers are calibrated, that is,
if the stated probabilities match frequencies, and checking calibration needs labels. In deployment,
labels are costly, late or missing: outcomes arrive weeks later or never, some questions have no
single right answer, and new questions are written faster than labelled evaluation sets can be
built. This paper asks what the law of the answers and the logical structure of the questions,
without any label, can refute about calibration, and whether the refutation can be made
statistically usable: valid at a finite sample, computable, and not broken by rounding or noise.

The direction of the question matters. Coherence does not certify calibration: a predictor whose
answers are always coherent passes every coherence check, however unrelated its answers are to the
label (Counterexample~\ref{cx:coherent}). Nor does incoherence measure marginal miscalibration:
marginal calibration implies coherence only on average (Lemma~\ref{lem:mean-coherence}), answers can
be marginally calibrated and still violate identities on every input
(Counterexample~\ref{cx:pointwise}), and so the documentation's claim of calibration need not
conflict with its advice against arithmetic identities. What we construct are therefore lower
bounds, \emph{certificates} that calibration is at least this bad, and a certificate of zero refutes
nothing.

Which calibration notion a certificate refutes depends on what the comparison of probabilities with
frequencies conditions on, and the notions differ in value, not only in definition. Ask about an
event $A$ and its complement with equal weights, and let the answers $(F_A, F_{\neg A})$ take the
values $(0, \tfrac12)$, $(1, \tfrac12)$, $(0, \tfrac34)$ and $(1, \tfrac14)$ with probability
$\tfrac14$ each. The average answers are coherent, and nothing can be refuted about calibration on
average. Whatever the labels, the answers are miscalibrated by at least $\tfrac1{16}$ when each
answer is conditioned on its own value (marginal calibration) and by at least $\tfrac3{16}$ when it
is conditioned on the whole pair (joint calibration), and no larger bounds follow from the law of
the answers (Theorem~\ref{thm:separation}). The average distance of the answers to the coherent set
is $\tfrac3{16}$, so an audit that reports it as the degree of miscalibration claims three times
what can be proved about marginal calibration. We call a label-free lower bound \emph{sharp} when no
larger one follows from what is observable: it is the least value of the residual over all joint
laws of answers and labels that are compatible with the law of the answers and the logical
structure. This is the sense of a sharp bound in partial identification \citep{manski2003partial};
it has nothing to do with the sharpness of a predictive distribution (its concentration), which
forecasters maximise subject to calibration \citep{gneiting2007probabilistic}.

Section~\ref{sec:identification} identifies these bounds in general. For every restriction on the
information that a bettor's stakes may use, an information-restricted minimax theorem
(Theorem~\ref{thm:minimax}) equates, for a finitely supported law of the answers, the least
calibration residual over the compatible label laws with the largest expected profit of a bettor who
settles every input in its worst world (a Dutch book without outcomes). Constant stakes, stakes on a
question's own answer and stakes on the whole bundle give the sharp bounds on the mean, marginal and
joint residuals, which the example above separates, and a bound on a bundle cannot be attributed to
a fixed question without assumptions on the others (Proposition~\ref{prop:attribution}).

Section~\ref{sec:stability} asks whether a certificate is stable. A certificate used to monitor a
predictor should not jump when the answers move a little, but the sharp marginal bound does: on a
two-point example it jumps from $0$ to above $\tfrac14$ under an arbitrarily small perturbation, and
rounding the answers to two decimals sends it back (Proposition~\ref{prop:discontinuity}). The jump
needs a logical constraint among the questions (Lemma~\ref{lem:no-constraint}), and no label-free
lower bound that is continuous in the Wasserstein distance between laws of answers stays within a
constant factor of the sharp one (Corollary~\ref{cor:closed-form}). Restricting the stakes to
$H$-Lipschitz functions of their own answer gives a bound $L_H$ that is $(1+H)$-Lipschitz in the
Wasserstein distance between laws of answers, that is sharp for a smooth calibration residual
$\Gamma_H$ rather than for the marginal calibration error, and that, for every $H > 0$, is positive
exactly when the sharp marginal bound is (Theorem~\ref{thm:stable}, Corollary~\ref{cor:zero-set}).
The two adjectives of our title therefore meet in $L_H$, which is sharp for $\Gamma_H$ and stable.
For the marginal calibration error $\Theta_w$ they cannot meet (Corollary~\ref{cor:closed-form}).

Section~\ref{sec:computation} makes $L_H$ computable from an i.i.d.\ stream of bundles. Stakes
represented by their values at fixed nodes, learnt by projected online gradient ascent and fixed
before each bundle is observed, give fixed-horizon lower confidence bounds, whose shortfall from
$L_H$ is, with probability at least $1 - \alpha$, bounded by a grid, a learning and a statistical
term (Theorem~\ref{thm:fixed-t}), and the same stakes in a betting process give anytime-valid ones
(Proposition~\ref{prop:anytime}). Section~\ref{sec:experiments} checks the mechanism on synthetic
data and reports a preregistered study of four predictors on two public classification data sets (a
commercial decision model through its API, an open-weight decision model and its base model, and a
zero-shot NLI classifier). All seven confirmatory certificates were positive, from $0.029$ to
$0.194$; the eighth pair of predictor and data set did not meet the preregistered pilot criterion
for collecting confirmation data.

\emph{Contributions.} The techniques (linear programming duality, a minimax theorem, projected
online gradient ascent, the Azuma--Hoeffding inequality and betting) are standard. Our contribution
is to state the calibration notions, what is achievable without labels, the price of stability and
the guarantees of the implementation for one object.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \emph{What is refutable.} Theorem~\ref{thm:minimax} brings four lines of work under one
  label-free minimax. For finitely supported laws, Corollary~\ref{cor:special} recovers, as special
  cases, results on measures of incoherence \citep{debona2015measuring}, on feasible joint
  posteriors \citep{arieli2021feasible} and on the mutual calibration of forecasters
  \citep{kong2026calibration}, and the stages of Corollary~\ref{cor:stages} are the refutation side
  of labelled hierarchies of calibration \citep{resin2026hierarchies,dwork2021outcome}. The equality
  is finite duality, and label-free partial identification of calibration error is not new
  \citep{kong2026calibration}. The closest work, \citet{andrews2026dutch}, measures the incoherence
  of language models by Dutch books, without a theoretical link to calibration error. The
  joint-stage measure, the distance of a bundle to the coherent set, is a known measure of
  incoherence \citep{debona2015measuring}; we read its expectation, for finitely supported laws, as
  the sharp label-free lower bound on the joint calibration error, below which lie the marginal and
  mean stages. What is new is a single minimax for bundles of different, logically related events
  and, on such bundles, the strict separation of the stages and the impossibility of attributing a
  bound to a given question.
  \item \emph{Stability and its price.} The discontinuity of the sharp marginal bound survives the
  minimisation over the compatible label laws, is produced by the logical constraints and admits no
  stable approximation within a uniform constant factor, while $L_H$ is stable, sharp for $\Gamma_H$
  and, for every $H > 0$, positive for exactly the laws under which marginal calibration is
  refutable without labels in the population. These results have labelled analogues
  \citep{blasiok2023unifying,gopalan2026importance}; ours concern the label-free, partially
  identified quantity.
  \item \emph{Certificates and evidence.} We give fixed-horizon and anytime-valid certificates for
  the same target; for the fixed-horizon certificate with stakes learnt by projected online gradient
  ascent, the shortfall is split into three terms, while the anytime certificate claims no rate. We
  also report a preregistered study on real predictors in which every confirmatory certificate was
  positive.
\end{enumerate}

\emph{What a certificate is about.} Every certificate in this paper concerns unconditional events
about one input and one label with finitely many values; on real data, reading the probabilities of
a choice query this way rests on its options exhausting the labels (Section~\ref{sec:limitations}).
It bounds a total over the bundle with weights fixed in advance that sum to one, so it bounds a
weighted average of per-question errors, not the error of any one question
(Proposition~\ref{prop:attribution}) and not that of all answers pooled into one sequence
(Section~\ref{sec:setup}). It is computed from the answers as the predictor returns them, without
rounding. A predictor whose answers are rounded, by its vendor or by an auditor, is a different
predictor with a different residual, and rounding can move the exact marginal bound discontinuously
(Proposition~\ref{prop:discontinuity}). Finally, each certificate is a lower bound on a named
residual. $L_0$, $L_{\mathrm{marg}}$ and $L_{\mathrm{joint}}$ are sharp for the mean, marginal and
joint residuals ($L_{\mathrm{joint}}$ for finitely supported laws), and $L_{\mathrm{joint}}$ does
not bound the marginal calibration error $\Theta_w$ (Counterexample~\ref{cx:pointwise}). $L_H$ and
its computable version $L_{H,G}$ are lower bounds on $\Theta_w$, and so, at their stated levels, are
the confidence bounds on $L_{H,G}$; $L_H$ is sharp for the smooth residual $\Gamma_H$, not for
$\Theta_w$. Values of these bounds computed on the empirical law of a sample are not certificates
(Appendix~\ref{app:descriptive}).

\section{Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\emph{Bundles and possible worlds.} A query-conditioned probabilistic predictor receives an input
together with a query and returns a probability. For one input we ask $m$ event queries and collect
the answers in a \emph{bundle} $F = (F_1, \dots, F_m) \in [0,1]^m$. Each queried event $B_i$ is a
function of a label $Y$ that takes finitely many values and is never observed. A \emph{possible
world} $\ell \in \mathcal{W}$ is a value of the label, with indicator vector $z^\ell =
(\mathbf{1}\{\ell \in B_i\})_{i \le m} \in \{0,1\}^m$; the realised indicator vector is $Z = z^Y$. A
\emph{choice query}, which returns a distribution over a set of options, enters the bundle as one
component per option. The \emph{coherent polytope}
\[
  \mathcal{C} = \operatorname{conv}\{z^\ell : \ell \in \mathcal{W}\}
\]
is the set of vectors $(\mu(B_1), \dots, \mu(B_m))$ obtained from probability measures $\mu$ on
$\mathcal{W}$, so a bundle is coherent exactly when it lies in $\mathcal{C}$.

Without labels one observes the law $P_F$ of the bundle and the logical structure $\{z^\ell\}$,
nothing else. We write $\mathcal{P}(P_F)$ for the set of joint laws $P$ of $(F, Z)$ on $[0,1]^m
\times \{z^\ell : \ell \in \mathcal{W}\}$ whose first marginal is $P_F$; the conditional law of $Z$
given $F$ is unrestricted. Each component carries a weight $w_i > 0$, with $\sum_i w_i = 1$, fixed
in advance with the bundle according to the role of its query: a choice query, an \emph{atom} $\{Y =
k\}$, a \emph{complement} $\{Y \ne k\}$ or a \emph{union} of labels. When certificates that use
fewer queries are compared with one another, each is computed on the same bundle and weights, with
zero stakes on the components it does not use, so that all of them bound the same residual. We use
the weighted $\ell_1$ distance $\operatorname{dist}^w_1(v, \mathcal{C}) = \min_{c \in \mathcal{C}}
\sum_i w_i \lvert v_i - c_i \rvert$ and the weighted Wasserstein distance $W_{1,w}(P, Q) =
\inf_{\gamma \in \Pi(P, Q)} \mathbb{E}_\gamma \sum_i w_i \lvert F_i - F_i' \rvert$ between laws of
bundles.

\emph{Semantics.} Every component asks an unconditional event about the same input and the same
label. We assume that the options of a choice query exhaust the possible labels and that a union is
asked as the explicit disjunction of its labels. These assumptions fix the semantics that the
logical structure encodes; a relation entered wrongly into $\mathcal{C}$ makes a statistically valid
certificate refute the wrong thing, while weakening a relation enlarges $\mathcal{C}$ and can only
lower the population bounds defined below.

\emph{Calibration residuals.} Calibration compares stated probabilities with frequencies, and the
comparison depends on what it conditions on. For sub-$\sigma$-algebras $\mathcal{H}_i \subseteq
\sigma(F)$ we define the \emph{information-restricted calibration residual}
\[
  \Gamma_{\mathcal{H}}(P) = \sum_{i=1}^m w_i \, \mathbb{E}\bigl\lvert \mathbb{E}[F_i - Z_i \mid
  \mathcal{H}_i] \bigr\rvert .
\]
The trivial $\sigma$-algebra gives the \emph{mean} residual $\sum_i w_i \lvert \mathbb{E}(F_i - Z_i)
\rvert$. The choice $\mathcal{H}_i = \sigma(F_i)$ gives the \emph{marginal} calibration error
\[
  \Theta_w(P) = \sum_{i=1}^m w_i \, \mathrm{ECE}_1(F_i), \qquad
  \mathrm{ECE}_1(F_i) = \mathbb{E}\bigl\lvert F_i - \Pr(Z_i = 1 \mid F_i) \bigr\rvert ,
\]
in which every component is conditioned on its own value.\footnote{Terminology varies. Our marginal
stage conditions each component on its own value; for the classes of a classifier this is class-wise
calibration, which \citet{kumar2019verified} and \citet{marx2023calibration} also call marginal
calibration. In probabilistic forecasting, marginal calibration is the agreement of the average
predictive distribution with the marginal law of the outcome
\citep{gneiting2007probabilistic,resin2026hierarchies}; for an event it is our mean stage.
\citet{andrews2026dutch} use marginal and joint for single and compound events.} The choice
$\mathcal{H}_i = \sigma(F)$ gives the \emph{joint} calibration error $\mathbb{E} \sum_i w_i \lvert
F_i - \Pr(Z_i = 1 \mid F) \rvert$, in which every component is conditioned on the whole bundle.
Because conditional expectation contracts, the three residuals, which we call the mean, marginal and
joint \emph{stages}, are ordered: mean $\le$ marginal $\le$ joint for every $P$. $\Theta_w$ is a
weighted average of per-component errors with fixed weights, not the expected calibration error of
all answers pooled into one sequence. If the pooled sequence draws the component of each answer
independently with probabilities $w_i$, Jensen's inequality makes its error at most $\Theta_w$, so a
lower bound on $\Theta_w$ is not one on the pooled error; with any other pooling the two are not
ordered.

Conditioning on an exact value makes $\Theta_w$ jump under arbitrarily small perturbations of the
answers. With the class $\mathcal{U}_H$ of stakes $u = (u_1, \dots, u_m)$ whose components $u_i
\colon [0,1] \to [-1,1]$ are $H$-Lipschitz, the \emph{smooth residual} is
\[
  \Gamma_H(P) = \sup_{u \in \mathcal{U}_H} \mathbb{E} \sum_{i=1}^m w_i \, u_i(F_i)\,(F_i - Z_i),
\]
the weight family of smooth calibration error \citep{blasiok2023unifying} applied component by
component. $\Gamma_H$ is nondecreasing in $H$, $\Gamma_0$ is the mean residual and $\Gamma_H \le
\Theta_w$.

\emph{Sharp label-free lower bounds.} A \emph{label-free lower bound} on a residual $\Gamma$ is a
functional $L$ of $P_F$, the logical structure and the weights with $L(P_F) \le \Gamma(P)$ for every
$P \in \mathcal{P}(P_F)$. It is \emph{sharp} when $L(P_F) = \inf_{P \in \mathcal{P}(P_F)}
\Gamma(P)$: no larger lower bound follows from what is observable. A certificate is such a lower
bound, or a finite-sample lower confidence bound for one; it can only show that calibration is at
least this bad.

\emph{Dutch books without outcomes.} A bettor who stakes $u_i$ on event $B_i$ at the price $F_i$
earns, as the seller, $\sum_i w_i u_i (F_i - Z_i)$. The outcome is not observed, so the bettor
counts the worst world:
\[
  d^w_u(F) = \min_{\ell \in \mathcal{W}} \sum_{i=1}^m w_i \, u_i(F) \, (F_i - z^\ell_i) \in [-1, 1]
  \qquad (\lvert u_i \rvert \le 1).
\]
The information a stake may use decides which calibration notion it tests. We write
$\mathcal{U}_{\mathcal{H}}$ for the stakes whose component $u_i$ is $\mathcal{H}_i$-measurable with
$\lvert u_i \rvert \le 1$; constant stakes ($\mathcal{U}_0$, which is also $\mathcal{U}_H$ with $H =
0$), stakes on the own value $u_i(F_i)$ ($\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{marg}}$) and stakes on the whole
bundle $u(F)$ ($\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{joint}}$) correspond to the mean, marginal and joint residuals.
Negative values of $d^w_u(F)$ are averaged as they are: clipping each value at zero would overstate
the expected profit, so only a final lower confidence bound is clipped.

\section{What Is Refutable Without Labels}
\label{sec:identification}

This section asks what the law of the bundle and its logical structure can refute about each
calibration residual. Section~\ref{sec:calibration-coherence} ties calibration to coherence and
marks where the tie ends. Section~\ref{sec:identification-results} identifies, for finitely
supported laws, the sharp label-free lower bound on every information-restricted residual, separates
the mean, marginal and joint stages on a small example, and shows that a bound on the bundle cannot
be attributed to a fixed question. The proofs are in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs-identification}.

\subsection{Calibration and Coherence}
\label{sec:calibration-coherence}

If every answer is marginally calibrated, the average answers are the frequencies of the queried
events, and these frequencies come from one probability measure.

\begin{lemma}[Marginal calibration implies coherence on average]
\label{lem:mean-coherence}
If $\Pr(Z_i = 1 \mid F_i) = F_i$ almost surely for every $i$, then $\mathbb{E}F \in \mathcal{C}$; in
particular every linear equality or inequality satisfied by all probability measures holds for
$(\mathbb{E}F_1, \dots, \mathbb{E}F_m)$. The converse fails.
\end{lemma}

Marginal calibration and coherence therefore meet only on average. A marginally calibrated predictor
can answer a question and its negation with probabilities that do not sum to one on an individual
input, while an identity or an inequality that fails on average, such as $\mathbb{E}F_1 >
\mathbb{E}F_2$ for $B_1 \subseteq B_2$, refutes marginal calibration. The converse fails twice over:
a predictor whose average answers are coherent can be miscalibrated under its true law
(Counterexample~\ref{cx:coherent}), and Theorem~\ref{thm:separation} gives a law of bundles with a
coherent average for which no compatible label law makes the answers marginally calibrated. In the
other direction, pointwise incoherence does not by itself imply marginal miscalibration.

\begin{counterexample}[Pointwise incoherence is not marginal miscalibration]
\label{cx:pointwise}
Let $A$ be an event and let the bundle $(F_A, F_{\neg A})$ take the values $(0, \tfrac12)$ and $(1,
\tfrac12)$ with probability $\tfrac12$ each, $A$ occurring exactly when $F_A = 1$. Then $\Theta_w =
0$, while $\mathbb{E}\operatorname{dist}^w_1(F, \mathcal{C}) = \tfrac14$ with equal weights.
\end{counterexample}

Counting coherence violations, or averaging the distance of each bundle to $\mathcal{C}$, does not
measure marginal calibration error, and an audit that reports either as the degree to which marginal
calibration is broken is refuted by this example. The pointwise distance bounds the joint
calibration error (Corollary~\ref{cor:stages}); here the joint calibration error is $\tfrac14$ as
well.

\begin{counterexample}[Coherent but miscalibrated]
\label{cx:coherent}
A predictor whose bundle always lies in $\mathcal{C}$ violates no coherence check, however unrelated
its answers are to the label. Every population certificate of this paper is then zero while
$\Theta_w$ can be large. A certificate of zero therefore means ``not refuted'', never
``calibrated''.
\end{counterexample}

Every result below is subject to this limit. A label-free check sees only the distortions that push
answers out of $\mathcal{C}$; an error in a coherent belief, however large, leaves no trace in $P_F$
and the logical structure. A positive certificate refutes, on its bundle, the calibration notion
whose residual it bounds (a finite-sample one at its level).

\subsection{Identification}
\label{sec:identification-results}

The sharp label-free lower bound on a residual $\Gamma_{\mathcal{H}}$ is, by definition, its infimum
over the label laws compatible with $P_F$: the smallest error under the label laws that a label-free
observer cannot rule out. A bettor gives lower bounds on it. If stakes that use only the information
$\mathcal{H}_i$ on $B_i$ make a positive expected profit when every input is settled in its worst
world, the answers cannot be calibrated in the sense of $\mathcal{H}$: under every compatible law
that expected profit is at most $\Gamma_{\mathcal{H}}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:weak-duality}). The next
theorem gives the converse: a calibration violation that no admissible bet extracts is absent under
some compatible label law.

\begin{theorem}[Information-restricted minimax]
\label{thm:minimax}
If $P_F$ has finite support, then
\[
  \inf_{P \in \mathcal{P}(P_F)} \Gamma_{\mathcal{H}}(P) = \sup_{u \in \mathcal{U}_{\mathcal{H}}}
  \mathbb{E}\bigl[d^w_u(F)\bigr],
\]
both sides are attained, and they are the optimal values of a finite linear program and its dual.
\end{theorem}

The primal chooses, with $P_F$ held fixed, the label law under which the predictor is as calibrated
as it can be; the dual chooses stakes that use only the permitted information and hedge against
every world. The equality is the duality of a finite linear program. For one event put to several
agents, \citet{arieli2021feasible} characterise feasible joint posteriors by a no-trade condition
and note that, for finitely supported laws, their characterisation reduces to Farkas' lemma; the
same finite duality gives the value of the marginal stage (Corollary~\ref{cor:special}(a)). What the
theorem adds is a single minimax for every information restriction on a bundle of different,
logically related events, so that the mean, marginal and joint stages, and any stage between them,
are one object. An attaining law shows that under some label law consistent with the observations
the predictor is calibrated up to the bound; it does not say that the predictor's actual errors
resemble those under that law. At the marginal stage a stake on $B_i$ must be the same on all inputs
at which $F_i$ takes the same value, and this coupling across inputs is what separates
$L_{\mathrm{marg}}$ from the pointwise distance.

\begin{corollary}[Three stages]
\label{cor:stages}
Taking $\mathcal{H}_i$ trivial, $\sigma(F_i)$ and $\sigma(F)$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:minimax} gives the
sharp label-free lower bounds
\[
  L_0 = \operatorname{dist}^w_1(\mathbb{E}F, \mathcal{C}), \qquad
  L_{\mathrm{marg}}, \qquad
  L_{\mathrm{joint}} = \mathbb{E} \operatorname{dist}^w_1(F, \mathcal{C})
\]
on the mean, marginal and joint residuals, where $L_{\mathrm{marg}}$ is the value of the linear
program; and $L_0 \le L_{\mathrm{marg}} \le L_{\mathrm{joint}}$. In particular $L_{\mathrm{marg}}
\le \Theta_w(P)$ for every $P \in \mathcal{P}(P_F)$.
\end{corollary}

The three bounds answer three questions. $L_0$ is the best test by the supporting hyperplanes of
$\mathcal{C}$, inequalities as well as identities: if $B_1 \subseteq B_2$ and $\mathbb{E}F = (0.8,
0.2)$, no identity is violated but the inclusion is, and $L_0 = 0.3$ with equal weights.
$L_{\mathrm{joint}}$ needs no learning; it averages the distance of each bundle to $\mathcal{C}$.
$L_{\mathrm{marg}}$ lies between them and needs the linear program, because its stakes are shared
across inputs. A bound grows with the information its stakes may use, and so does the notion it
bounds: a larger bound refutes a stronger notion, not the same notion more strongly. The stages
order calibration notions by the $\sigma$-algebra they condition on, as labelled hierarchies of
calibration do \citep{resin2026hierarchies}, and the information available to a stake plays the role
of the access of a distinguisher in outcome indistinguishability \citep{dwork2021outcome};
Theorem~\ref{thm:minimax} is the label-free, refutation side of that correspondence.

Theorem~\ref{thm:minimax} also contains, as special cases, results and quantities from three other
lines of work: the feasibility of joint posterior beliefs, measures of incoherence, and the mutual
calibration of forecasters.

\begin{corollary}[Special cases]
\label{cor:special}
Let $P_F$ have finite support.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item[(a)] \emph{One event asked $m$ times.} If $B_1 = \dots = B_m = A$ with $A$ neither sure nor
  impossible, then
  \[
    L_{\mathrm{marg}} = \sup_{a} \, \mathbb{E}\Bigl[\sum_{i=1}^m a_i(F_i)\,F_i - \max\Bigl\{0,
    \sum_{i=1}^m a_i(F_i)\Bigr\}\Bigr]
  \]
  over measurable $a_i \colon [0,1] \to [-w_i, w_i]$. Hence $L_{\mathrm{marg}} = 0$ if and only if
  $F \equiv 0^m$, $F \equiv 1^m$, or $P_F$ is the law of the posterior beliefs about $A$ of $m$
  agents with a common prior $p \in (0,1)$: the no-trade characterisation of feasible joint
  posteriors \citep[Theorem~3]{arieli2021feasible}; for $m = 2$, Arieli et al.\ state an equivalent
  characterisation due to \citet{dawid1995coherent}.
  \item[(b)] \emph{The joint stage, pointwise.} For every $v \in [0,1]^m$,
  \[
    \operatorname{dist}^w_1(v, \mathcal{C}) = \max_{u \in [-1,1]^m} \min_{\ell \in \mathcal{W}}
    \sum_{i=1}^m w_i u_i (v_i - z^\ell_i),
  \]
  the identity between distance-based and Dutch-book measures of incoherence
  \citep{debona2015measuring}; $L_{\mathrm{joint}}$ is its expectation.
  \item[(c)] \emph{Two forecasters of one label.} Let $Q_1, Q_2 \in \Delta_K$ forecast a label $Y
  \in \{1, \dots, K\}$, written as a one-hot vector. Form the bundle $F = (Q_1, Q_2)$ of the $2K$
  events $\{Y = k\}$ with weights $1/(2K)$, and give coordinate $(j, k)$ the information
  $\sigma(Q_j)$. Then $\inf_{P \in \mathcal{P}(P_F)} \Gamma_{\mathcal{H}}(P) = \mathrm{MinECE}/K$,
  where
  \[
    \mathrm{MinECE} = \tfrac12 \inf_{P \in \mathcal{P}(P_F)} \mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert Q_1 -
    \mathbb{E}[Y \mid Q_1] \rVert_1 + \lVert Q_2 - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid Q_2] \rVert_1\bigr]
  \]
  is the minimal calibration error of \citet{kong2026calibration}; so $\mathrm{MinECE} = K \sup_u
  \mathbb{E}[d^w_u(F)]$ over stakes $u_{(j,k)} = u_{jk}(Q_j) \in [-1, 1]$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{corollary}

Case~(a) turns the no-trade condition into a value: $L_{\mathrm{marg}}$ is the least marginal
calibration error that a label law compatible with forecasts of one event must leave, and its zero
set is the feasibility characterisation, apart from the two degenerate laws, which pass the no-trade
test without an interior prior. Case~(b) is the identity behind distance-based measures of
incoherence; what Corollary~\ref{cor:stages} adds is that its expectation is the sharp label-free
lower bound on the joint calibration error, and Counterexample~\ref{cx:pointwise} shows that it does
not bound the marginal one. \citet[Appendix~A]{andrews2026dutch} bound the stakes in $\ell_1$
instead and obtain the distance in the supremum norm, the dual of $\ell_1$. We bound each stake
separately, and then, under a fixed label law, the best expected profit against the realised
outcomes separates across components: the stakes $u_i = \operatorname{sign} \mathbb{E}[F_i - Z_i
\mid \mathcal{H}_i]$ make the second inequality of Lemma~\ref{lem:weak-duality} an equality, so that
this profit is the weighted sum $\Gamma_{\mathcal{H}}$ of the per-component residuals, each
conditioned on its own information. In case~(c) a coordinate is conditioned on the whole forecast
vector of its forecaster. This information contains the marginal one and is contained in the joint
one, so $L_{\mathrm{marg}} \le \mathrm{MinECE}/K \le L_{\mathrm{joint}}$; for $K = 2$ it is the
marginal stage. \citet{kong2026calibration} bound the arbitrage of zero-mean trades, each depending
only on its forecaster's own forecast and with payoffs in $[-1, 1]$, between $\mathrm{MinECE}$ and
$2\,\mathrm{MinECE}$; bounding the stakes instead of the payoffs, as $d^w_u$ does, turns the bracket
into an equality.

The next example, small enough to check by hand, separates the three stages. It mixes the two inputs
of Counterexample~\ref{cx:pointwise}, which a marginally calibrated law can produce, with two inputs
that no such law can.

\begin{theorem}[Four-point separation]
\label{thm:separation}
For an event $A$ and its complement with equal weights, let $(F_A, F_{\neg A})$ take the values $(0,
\tfrac12)$, $(1, \tfrac12)$, $(0, \tfrac34)$ and $(1, \tfrac14)$ with probability $\tfrac14$ each.
Then $0 = L_0 < L_{\mathrm{marg}} = \tfrac1{16} < L_{\mathrm{joint}} = \tfrac3{16}$.
\end{theorem}

Table~\ref{tab:four-point} lists a label law that attains $L_{\mathrm{marg}}$ and stakes that earn
it, so the separation can be checked without a solver (Figure~\ref{fig:four-point}). On these
answers the average distance to $\mathcal{C}$, $\tfrac3{16}$, is three times the marginal
calibration error that can be proved without labels, $\tfrac1{16}$, and an audit's conclusion
depends on which of the two it reports. The marginal bound can also be zero while the joint one is
not. On a fair die, let a choice query over the six faces return $0.83$ for a uniformly drawn face
and $0.034$ for each other face, beside atom queries $\{Y = k\}$ that always answer $\tfrac16$. The
choice query is overconfident, yet $L_{\mathrm{marg}} = 0$: under the label law in which the drawn
face comes up with probability $0.83$ and each other face with probability $0.034$, every component
is marginally calibrated. $L_{\mathrm{joint}} > 0$ because the two queries disagree on the same
event at every input. That the roll does not depend on the drawn face is information beyond $P_F$
and the logical structure.

A certificate bounds an error summed over the bundle. In practice one often cares about one
question, the target, and asks the others only to check it.

\begin{proposition}[No attribution to a fixed target]
\label{prop:attribution}
Split the components into targets $J$ and auxiliaries $O = \{1, \dots, m\} \setminus J$, and let
$\mathcal{P}_J(P_{F_J})$ be the analogue of $\mathcal{P}(P_F)$ for the bundle $F_J$ alone, whose
worlds are the restrictions $z^\ell_J$. With no restriction on the auxiliary answers,
\[
  \inf_{P \in \mathcal{P}(P_F)} \sum_{i \in J} w_i \, \mathrm{ECE}_1(F_i) =
  \inf_{P \in \mathcal{P}_J(P_{F_J})} \sum_{i \in J} w_i \, \mathrm{ECE}_1(F_i) :
\]
observing $F_O$ does not lower-bound the targets' error any further. If $J = \{i\}$ and component
$i$ asks an event that is neither sure nor impossible, both sides are $0$.
\end{proposition}

When the answers to ``$A$?'' and ``not $A$?'' sum to $1.19$ on average, so that $L_0 > 0$, the
bundle is refuted, but nothing in $P_F$ says which answer is wrong: a label law under which the
target is calibrated and the auxiliary answer carries all the error is always compatible. What a
lower bound $L \le \Theta_w$ says about single questions is that $\mathrm{ECE}_1(F_i) \ge L$ for at
least one component, since $\Theta_w$ is a weighted average. This covers $L_0$, $L_{\mathrm{marg}}$,
$L_H$ and $L_{H,G}$ and, on the events where they hold, finite-sample lower confidence bounds on
them; it does not cover $L_{\mathrm{joint}}$ or another bound from Theorem~\ref{thm:minimax} that
conditions on more than a component's own value, such as $\mathrm{MinECE}/K$ in
Corollary~\ref{cor:special}(c), which can be positive while every $\mathrm{ECE}_1(F_i)$ is zero
under the true law (Appendix~\ref{app:proofs-identification}). Attributing the bound to a given
target needs explicit assumptions on the auxiliaries, such as bounds on their calibration errors,
which we do not pursue. For the same reason, certificates of parts of a bundle do not add up. With
weights $\tfrac12$ each, the answer $0.8$ to ``$A$?'' alone, or to ``not $A$?'' alone, refutes
nothing, while the two answers together give $L_0 = 0.3$. Nor is the certificate a submodular
function of the set of queries, so choosing queries greedily comes with no guarantee.

\section{Stability and Its Price}
\label{sec:stability}

A certificate used to monitor a predictor should not jump when the answers move a little, by
rounding, by noise or between two runs of the same model. This section shows that the sharp bound on
the marginal calibration error can jump, traces the jump to the logical constraints of the bundle,
gives the price of stability in closed form, and shows that, for every law of the answers, the
stable bound $L_H$ is the sharp label-free lower bound on the smooth residual $\Gamma_H$ and, for
every $H > 0$, is positive exactly when the sharp bound on $\Theta_w$ is. The proofs are in
Appendix~\ref{app:proofs-stability}.

For a general $P_F$ we set
\[
  L_{\mathrm{marg}}(P_F) = \inf_{P \in \mathcal{P}(P_F)} \Theta_w(P) , \qquad
  L_H(P_F) = \sup_{u \in \mathcal{U}_H} \mathbb{E}[d^w_u(F)] ;
\]
$L_0$ and $L_{\mathrm{joint}}$ keep the formulas of Corollary~\ref{cor:stages}. Since a stake in
$\mathcal{U}_H$ is a function of its own component, Lemma~\ref{lem:weak-duality} gives $L_H(P_F) \le
\Gamma_H(P) \le \Theta_w(P)$ for every $P \in \mathcal{P}(P_F)$, so $L_H$ is a label-free lower
bound on both residuals and $L_H \le L_{\mathrm{marg}}$.

\begin{proposition}[The exact marginal certificate is discontinuous]
\label{prop:discontinuity}
For $0 \le \varepsilon \le \tfrac12$ let $F^\varepsilon$ take $(0, \tfrac12 - \varepsilon)$ and $(1,
\tfrac12 + \varepsilon)$ with probability $\tfrac12$ each, as a bundle on an event and its
complement with equal weights. Then $L_{\mathrm{marg}}(P_{F^0}) = 0$ while, for $\varepsilon > 0$,
\[
  L_{\mathrm{marg}}(P_{F^\varepsilon}) = L_{\mathrm{joint}}(P_{F^\varepsilon}) = \tfrac14 +
  \tfrac{\varepsilon}2 , \qquad W_{1,w}(P_{F^\varepsilon}, P_{F^0}) = \tfrac{\varepsilon}2 .
\]
\end{proposition}

At $\varepsilon = 0$ this is Counterexample~\ref{cx:pointwise}: $F_{\neg A}$ is $\tfrac12$ on both
inputs, and a label law can pool the two inputs and calibrate it given its own value. For
$\varepsilon > 0$ the value of each component tells the two inputs apart, so conditioning a
component on its own value is conditioning on the whole bundle. Under every compatible label law the
marginal and joint residuals then coincide, and the marginal bound jumps to the joint one. The
second component is the predictor of \citet[Lemma~4.8]{blasiok2023unifying}, which answers $\tfrac12
- \varepsilon$ and $\tfrac12 + \varepsilon$ on two equally likely inputs with different labels and
shows that the expected calibration error is discontinuous at a calibrated predictor. There the
labels are observed. Here the jump survives the minimisation over every label law compatible with
$P_F$. It is a property of conditioning on exact values, not of the linear program: for $\varepsilon
< 0.005$, rounding the answers to two decimals maps $F^\varepsilon$ to $F^0$, and the exact marginal
bound drops from above $\tfrac14$ to $0$ (Figure~\ref{fig:two-point}).

With observed labels, the answers to a single question already show such a jump. Without labels they
cannot: the next lemma shows that a single question that is neither sure nor impossible is never
refuted, and that the jump needs a logical constraint among the queried events.

\begin{lemma}[No logical constraint, no jump]
\label{lem:no-constraint}
Let $S$ be the set of components whose event is sure or impossible, $z^\ell_i = c_i$ for every
world, and suppose the remaining events are logically independent: $\{(z^\ell_i)_{i \notin S} : \ell
\in \mathcal{W}\} = \{0,1\}^{\{1, \dots, m\} \setminus S}$. Then for every $P_F$ and every $H \ge
0$,
\[
  L_0 = L_{\mathrm{marg}} = L_{\mathrm{joint}} = L_H = \sum_{i \in S} w_i \, \mathbb{E}\lvert F_i -
  c_i \rvert ,
\]
which is $1$-Lipschitz in $W_{1,w}$. In particular a bundle of one query that is neither sure nor
impossible is never refuted, and a discontinuity such as that of
Proposition~\ref{prop:discontinuity} requires logical constraints among the nontrivial events.
\end{lemma}

Without such constraints, the label law that draws each nontrivial outcome as an independent coin
with the stated probability calibrates every nontrivial component, even jointly; for one prediction
this is the observation of \citet[Section~2]{gopalan2026importance} that drawing the label as a coin
with the stated probability yields a calibrated joint law of prediction and label. What remains is
the error of the answers to sure or impossible events, which no label law can remove and which moves
continuously with $P_F$. In Proposition~\ref{prop:discontinuity} the constraint that exactly one of
$A$ and $\neg A$ occurs ties the two components to one outcome: for $\varepsilon = 0$ some label law
still makes both marginally calibrated, and for $\varepsilon > 0$ none does. The jump of
$L_{\mathrm{marg}}$ is thus produced by the coherence constraints: without them none of the bounds
jumps, and the single constraint of a complement pair suffices.

\begin{corollary}[Closed form and the impossibility of a uniform constant factor]
\label{cor:closed-form}
In the setting of Proposition~\ref{prop:discontinuity}, for every $H \ge 0$,
\[
  L_H(P_{F^\varepsilon}) = \bigl(\tfrac14 + \tfrac{\varepsilon}2\bigr) \min\{1, H\varepsilon\} .
\]
Hence $L_H / L_{\mathrm{marg}} = \min\{1, H\varepsilon\} \to 0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$, and no
distribution-free constant $c_H > 0$ gives $L_H \ge c_H L_{\mathrm{marg}}$. More generally, no lower
bound that vanishes at $P_{F^0}$ and is continuous in $W_{1,w}$ admits such a constant.
\end{corollary}

On the two-point example a bettor profits only by staking differently on the two values $\tfrac12
\pm \varepsilon$ of $F_{\neg A}$. An $H$-Lipschitz stake can make the two stakes differ by at most
$2H\varepsilon$, against $2$ for an unrestricted one, so the profit shrinks by the factor $\min\{1,
H\varepsilon\}$. This is the price of stability, and no label-free lower bound on $\Theta_w$ that is
continuous in $W_{1,w}$ avoids it. A label-free lower bound on $\Theta_w$ is at most
$L_{\mathrm{marg}}$, so a nonnegative one vanishes at $P_{F^0}$; if it is continuous there, it is
small at $P_{F^\varepsilon}$ for small $\varepsilon$, where $L_{\mathrm{marg}} > \tfrac14$. With
observed labels, \citet[Lemmas~4.3 and~4.8]{blasiok2023unifying} together give the counterpart: a
calibration measure that vanishes on calibrated predictors and is Lipschitz in the predictor is not
bounded below by a constant multiple of the expected calibration error.
Corollary~\ref{cor:closed-form} gives the price in closed form for the label-free bound. On a finite
grid the price is bounded. If any two distinct values taken by the same component differ by at least
$\delta > 0$, then
\begin{equation}
  \min\{1, H\delta/2\} \, L_{\mathrm{marg}} \le L_H \le L_{\mathrm{marg}} ,
  \label{eq:finite-grid}
\end{equation}
so $L_H = L_{\mathrm{marg}}$ once $H \ge 2/\delta$ (Appendix~\ref{app:proofs-stability}). For
answers given to two decimals, $\delta \ge 0.01$, and $H = 200$ recovers the exact marginal bound,
at the stability constant $1 + H = 201$ of the next theorem.

\begin{theorem}[Stable certificate]
\label{thm:stable}
Let $F \in [0,1]^m$ have any law $P_F$ and fix $0 \le H < \infty$. Then
\[
  \inf_{P \in \mathcal{P}(P_F)} \Gamma_H(P) = \sup_{u \in \mathcal{U}_H} \mathbb{E}\bigl[d^w_u(F)
  \bigr] = L_H(P_F),
\]
the infimum is attained, and for two laws of bundles with the same logical structure, weights and
$H$,
\[
  \bigl\lvert L_H(P_F) - L_H(P_{F'}) \bigr\rvert \le (1 + H) \, W_{1,w}(P_F, P_{F'}) .
\]
\end{theorem}

Theorem~\ref{thm:minimax} rests on a finite linear program, which continuous answers do not give.
Restricting the stakes to $H$-Lipschitz functions keeps the minimax for every law of the answers, by
a compactness argument, and makes the bound move with the answers: a stake that cannot change
quickly earns about the same on nearby answers. For finitely supported laws, $L_H$ is again the
value of a finite linear program, in the values of the stakes at the support points under Lipschitz
constraints between neighbouring values (Lemma~\ref{lem:extension}); this is how we compute it. At
$H = 0$ the stakes are constants and $\Gamma_0$ is the mean residual, whose infimum over the
compatible label laws is $\operatorname{dist}^w_1(\mathbb{E}F, \mathcal{C})$ for every law
(Corollary~\ref{cor:stages} and its proof). So the theorem identifies $L_0$ with the value of the
best constant stake for every law, as Theorem~\ref{thm:minimax} did for finitely supported ones, and
the two meanings of $L_0$ (the formula and $L_H$ at $H = 0$) agree.

Two cautions. First, $L_H$ is sharp for the smooth residual $\Gamma_H$, not for $\Theta_w$: $L_H =
\inf_P \Gamma_H(P) \le \inf_P \Theta_w(P) = L_{\mathrm{marg}}$, with the gap of
Corollary~\ref{cor:closed-form}; this is the sense of ``sharp'' in our title. Second, the theorem
makes the population value stable. It does not say that a finite-sample bound, whose stakes are
learnt from the data, moves by at most $(1 + H)\,W_{1,w}$. With observed labels, the smooth
calibration error of one predictor, whose stakes are $1$-Lipschitz ($m = 1$, $H = 1$ in our
notation), is within a factor of two of its lower distance from calibration
\citep[Theorem~7.3]{blasiok2023unifying} and of its earth mover's distance to the set of calibrated
joint laws of prediction and label \citep[Lemma~2.5]{gopalan2026importance}; we do not carry that
factor to other $H$. The theorem instead identifies, without labels and for every $H$, the least
smooth residual over the compatible label laws; the equality itself follows from a minimax theorem.

\begin{corollary}[Stabilisation keeps what is refutable]
\label{cor:zero-set}
Let $F \in [0,1]^m$ have any law $P_F$ and fix $0 < H < \infty$. Then
\[
  L_H(P_F) = 0 \iff L_{\mathrm{marg}}(P_F) = 0 \iff \Theta_w(P) = 0 \text{ for some } P \in
  \mathcal{P}(P_F) .
\]
\end{corollary}

Corollary~\ref{cor:closed-form} says that stabilisation shrinks a bound;
Corollary~\ref{cor:zero-set} says that, for $H > 0$, it never shrinks a positive sharp bound on
$\Theta_w$ to zero. Lipschitz functions are dense among the continuous functions, so under a label
law at which no Lipschitz stake on a component's own value profits, no stake on that value profits
either. Stabilisation gives up a uniform constant factor but keeps, for every fixed $H > 0$, the set
of laws of the answers under which marginal calibration is refuted without labels in the population.
It says nothing about the sample size a refutation needs, which can be large when $L_H$ is small.
The result concerns the class $\mathcal{U}_H$ and does not give the finite class of
Section~\ref{sec:computation} the same zero set; it excludes $H = 0$; and the blind spot of
Counterexample~\ref{cx:coherent} remains, since $L_{\mathrm{marg}} = 0$ is not evidence that the
predictor is marginally calibrated under its true law. With observed labels, the smooth calibration
error of one predictor ($H = 1$) is likewise positive for every miscalibrated predictor, which
\citet[Table~1]{blasiok2023unifying} list as its soundness.
